articles.title: Move-Away Case
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A non-relocating parent has legal rights that may allow them to challenge a child's proposed move, request a custody hearing, and seek changes to an existing parenting arrangement. When one parent plans to move to another city or state with the child, the other parent does not necessarily lose their say in the decision. Courts often evaluate relocation disputes using the best interests of the child standard , considering how the move could affect the child's well-being. A move-away lawyer can help the non-relocating parent understand their legal options and take appropriate steps to protect their parental rights. Understanding the available legal protections can help a non-relocating parent respond before the move disrupts an established custody arrangement. The Right to Challenge a Child's Relocation One of the most important rights a non-relocating parent may have is the ability to object to a proposed move. Depending on the state's relocation laws and the existing custody order, the parent may ask the court to restrict the relocation. A parent should review the child custody agreement to determine whether advance notice or court approval is required. A move-away lawyer can explain the applicable requirements and help file an objection when there are valid legal grounds. The Right to Request a Court Hearing When parents cannot agree on relocation, the non-relocating parent may be able to request a court hearing. This allows both parents to present their positions and provide evidence about how the move could affect the child. Courts generally apply the best interests of the child standard when evaluating custody and relocation disputes, although the precise legal test varies by jurisdiction. A judge may consider: The child's relationship with each parent Educational needs Emotional well-being Existing custody arrangements The reasons for the proposed move An experienced move-away lawyer can help organize this evidence and present a clear argument focused on the child's needs rather than solely on the parents' disagreement. The Right to Seek Changes to Custody A proposed relocation may give the non-relocating parent grounds to ask the court to reconsider the current custody arrangement. Depending on state law, the parent may seek primary physical custody or a revised parenting schedule if the move would make the existing arrangement impractical. However, relocation does not automatically mean custody will change. The court will assess the circumstances and apply the relevant legal requirements before deciding whether a modification is appropriate. The Right to Request a Practical Visitation Plan If the court permits the relocation, the non-relocating parent may seek a revised visitation schedule to maintain a meaningful relationship with the child. This could include extended visits during school holidays, alternating holidays, transportation arrangements, and regular video calls. The court may consider travel costs, the child's age, school commitments, and each parent's ability to support continued contact. A move-away lawyer can help negotiate a realistic plan or ask the court to establish clear terms if the parents cannot reach an agreement. Legal Protections Under State Law Relocation rules vary across the United States. For example, California Family Code § 7501 addresses a custodial parent's ability to change a child's residence, subject to the court's authority to restrict a move that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. The application of this law depends on the custody arrangement and the circumstances of the case. Key Points to Remember A non-relocating parent may challenge a proposed move under applicable state law. The parent may request a hearing and present evidence supporting their position. Relocation may justify seeking a custody modification, depending on the circumstances. Revised visitation and travel arrangements can help preserve parent-child contact. A move-away lawyer can explain legal options and help protect parental rights throughout the process.

articles.title: CCTV Rules in Dubai
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Security cameras are standard in Dubai shops, warehouses and offices, yet many employers overlook the legal side. A camera that records staff is collecting personal data, and that changes how it must be planned, explained and managed. This article covers the main rules on employee monitoring in the UAE, from camera placement to footage storage. The Legal Framework Behind Workplace Cameras Two sets of rules matter. Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data treats identifiable images of people as personal data, so recorded footage falls within its scope. The UAE Data Office is named as the federal regulator. Businesses in the DIFC and ADGM follow their own data protection regimes instead. The second layer is local. In Dubai, Law No. 12 of 2016 regulates the security industry and created the Security Industry Regulatory Agency (SIRA), which licenses and supervises security service providers, including firms that install surveillance systems. Employers should check the current status of the federal law's executive regulations before finalising any policy. For a practical summary of how these layers fit together, this guide to CCTV rules in Dubai is a useful reference. Where Cameras Can and Cannot Go Placement should follow a genuine risk. Entrances, reception desks, cash points, safes, stockrooms and server rooms are usually easy to justify for security, safety or loss prevention. Wide shots of shared work areas can be reasonable if the purpose is disclosed to staff. Some spaces are off limits. Toilets, changing rooms, prayer rooms and private rest areas should never be filmed. A gym, for instance, may cover its reception and training floor but not its locker rooms. A camera trained on one employee's desk, or one that captures neighbouring units or public areas without good reason, is likely to be seen as excessive. Audio deserves special caution. Take legal advice before recording conversations. Clearly notified call recording in a defined customer service role is easier to defend than general office audio. Telling Staff and Writing a Policy Transparency is central. Put clear signs at entrances and in monitored zones stating that CCTV is in operation, why it is used and who to contact with questions. Repeat the same information in employment contracts or the staff handbook. A written monitoring policy should explain the purpose of each camera, the areas covered, and any monitoring of email, company devices or work systems. Ask each employee to acknowledge it in writing, and keep the policy consistent with UAE labour rules and your internal grievance process. Company accounts and devices are easier to monitor lawfully than personal ones. If personal devices are involved, set firm limits and obtain consent. Covert monitoring should be avoided unless legal advice supports it. Installing and Reviewing the System Start by mapping each camera to a specific risk. A logistics firm might justify two cameras at a loading bay after past theft. Then use a SIRA-licensed provider rather than fitting consumer cameras yourself, and keep installation records and a camera map. Give staff a fair way to raise objections. If an employee feels a camera is too close to their workstation, the complaint should go through the normal HR procedure and be reviewed on its merits. Review the setup periodically. Storing and Sharing Footage Securely Footage should sit in a secure system with access limited to named managers. Log every viewing and export, and set a fixed retention period that is applied consistently. Some activities carry minimum retention requirements, so confirm the rule for your sector with the relevant authority. Connected cameras also need protection: change default passwords, keep firmware updated, encrypt stored footage and place cameras on a network separate from office systems. When someone requests footage, confirm who they are and why they need it. Share it only for a lawful reason, such as a police request, record each disclosure and blur third parties where appropriate. Delete recordings once they are no longer needed. Conclusion Compliant workplace monitoring in Dubai rests on four principles: a clear purpose, proportionate coverage, open communication with staff and secure handling of footage. Documenting each decision makes recordings easier to rely on in a dispute. These principles apply across the emirate's business zones, including free zone companies such as those licensed in Meydan Free Zone , which should also confirm any premises rules with their landlord before installing cameras.

articles.title: Self-Defense Claim
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Confrontations can become dangerous in a matter of seconds. A person may have to decide whether someone poses a real threat before there is time to step back and think through every possible consequence. Later, however, that decision may be examined closely in court. Understanding self-defense laws Idaho follows can help a person to protect themselves or another person with reasonable force in certain circumstances. The law also says a person does not have to wait until they know with certainty that a danger is real before acting. Instead, the law considers whether the circumstances would have led a reasonable person to believe that immediate action was necessary. A Person Must Face an Imminent Threat Self-defense generally depends on the presence of an immediate danger. A person cannot claim self-defense simply because they were angry with someone or expected trouble at some point in the future. The circumstances must support a reasonable belief that harm was about to occur. The law allows a person to act based on appearances that would influence a reasonable person in the same situation. That means these rules do not require someone to wait for an attacker to confirm their intentions before responding. The Response Must Be Reasonable The amount of force used can matter greatly. Legal standards permit a person to use the force and means that would appear necessary to a reasonable person facing similar circumstances and possessing similar knowledge. This does not mean every response is automatically protected. The facts surrounding the confrontation matter. What did the person see? What did they know at the time? What was happening immediately before the force was used? Courts may examine those circumstances without relying solely on what became clear afterward. The Person Must Act Because of the Threat The use of force must be connected to the danger the person faced. Self-defense is generally tied to an imminent threat. It cannot be used simply to justify acting out of anger or another separate motive. For example, getting into an argument does not automatically make self-defense valid if the situation later becomes physical. What happened before the force was used still matters. What If the Person Defends Someone Else? The self-defense protections can extend to protecting another person. These rules allow someone to come to another person’s aid when they reasonably believe that person faces an imminent danger or certain serious crimes. The same basic concerns remain important. The person must have a reasonable basis to believe immediate action is needed, and the response must be appropriate to the circumstances. A person cannot simply assume that another individual is in danger without considering what was actually happening. Special Rules Apply to Homes and Other Locations Self-defense rules contain additional protections involving a habitation, place of business or employment, and occupied vehicles. Under certain circumstances, the law creates a presumption that a person acted reasonably when using force against someone who unlawfully enters or attempts to enter such a place in specified ways. Those rules can involve details about how the person entered, whether force or stealth was used, and whether the person appeared to be committing a felony. The specific facts matter. What If Deadly Force Is Used? Deadly force is treated more seriously under the law. Separate rules may apply when someone uses deadly force to protect themselves, another person, or their home. A person who was the initial aggressor may also face additional issues. The case law has recognized that an initial aggressor generally cannot rely on self-defense unless they first withdraw from the confrontation in good faith. That makes the events leading up to the confrontation important, rather than focusing only on the final moment. What Should You Do After a Self-Defense Incident? If you were involved in a confrontation where force was used, preserve relevant evidence and avoid assuming what the law will decide. Witness accounts, photographs, video footage, messages, medical records, and other evidence may help establish what happened. Self-defense questions can turn on small details. Where the people were standing, what was said, who acted first, and what each person knew at the time may all become relevant. If you are facing criminal charges after an incident involving claimed self-defense, getting legal advice early can help you understand how laws may apply to the facts of your case.

articles.title: Can a Virtual Office Help
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Melbourne is one of Australia's most competitive business markets, and your address matters more than most people expect. Clients form impressions before they've spoken a word to you, and a virtual office can shift those impressions in your favour without the cost of a full lease. The real question isn't whether a virtual office works. It's whether the right one, in the right location, can actually change how Melbourne clients respond to your business. What a Virtual Office Actually Gives You in Melbourne If you're trying to establish a business presence in Melbourne , a virtual office puts a premium CBD address on your business card, your website, your proposals, and your email footer - without requiring you to pay for a full-time physical space. That distinction carries real weight in a city where clients often Google your address before returning your call. A Collins Street or Bourke Street listing signals stability and professionalism in a way that a home suburb simply doesn't. This isn't a marketing point; it's a practical observation about how Melbourne's business culture actually works. Buyers here are accustomed to dealing with established firms in recognisable buildings, and a virtual office lets smaller operators, consultants, and interstate businesses compete on that same visual footing. The cost gap is significant - virtual office plans typically start well under $200 per month, compared to thousands for a leased CBD desk. A Professional Address Changes How Clients See You Melbourne's professional services market - legal, financial, consulting, and technology - runs heavily on trust. And trust, at the first point of contact, is partly visual. A prospect who finds your business listed at a respected CBD address reads that as evidence of scale and permanence, even if you run a lean remote operation. That assumption isn't irrational; it reflects how most established firms operate in this city. A virtual office lets you meet that expectation honestly, without overstating your size or infrastructure. You're not pretending to occupy a floor of a skyscraper, you're using a genuine address tied to a real building with real reception and mail handling. The practical effect: quotes, proposals, and cold outreach go out from an address that passes the Google Street View test. In a market where many buyers eliminate suppliers before a first conversation, that quiet credibility can stop your pitch from being screened out before it's even read. Mail Handling and Phone Answering That Keep You in the Room Beyond the address itself, virtual office arrangements typically include mail handling and professional call answering. So when a Melbourne prospect calls your listed number, a trained receptionist picks up in your business's name rather than sending them to a personal voicemail. That one detail changes the entire experience of contacting you. But the impact goes further than phone calls. Mail handling means legal correspondence, samples, or physical documents sent to your address get received, logged, and forwarded, which matters if you're operating remotely, interstate, or internationally. Most providers also give you access to meeting rooms at the same building on a casual basis, so you can take a client meeting in a proper boardroom when the occasion calls for it. You're not locked into a monthly desk commitment, but the option to show up in person is there when a face-to-face meeting would genuinely strengthen a deal. Honestly, that flexibility is one of the more underrated advantages of this model. How a Virtual Office Helps You Win Melbourne Business Landing Melbourne clients isn't purely a matter of having the right address. It also comes down to how you position yourself across the sales process, and a virtual office quietly supports several stages of that process at once. Credibility starts before the first conversation, it runs through your website footer, your email signature, how your calls get answered, and the physical space where you eventually meet. A virtual office strengthens most of those touchpoints without requiring you to change how you work day-to-day. The catch is that it works best when the address and the services behind it are genuinely premium; a low-cost address in a mediocre building doesn't carry the same weight as one in a well-known Melbourne tower. So the choice of provider and location within the CBD is worth sweating, not just the monthly price point. First Impressions in a Competitive Pitch Process Many Melbourne businesses make shortlisting decisions based on surface signals before they've done any real due diligence. A competitor who lists a CBD address, answers calls professionally, and sends proposals from a recognised building gets further into shortlists than an equally capable operator working from home. That's not fair, and it's no reflection of actual quality - but it's how competitive markets behave. A virtual office lets you control those surface signals without misrepresenting anything about your business. You're genuinely associated with that address: your mail arrives there, your calls are answered there, your clients can meet you there. So when a prospective Melbourne client does their research, what they find lines up with what you've told them. Consistency builds confidence. And in a city full of options, confidence is often what pushes a prospect from "maybe" to a signed agreement - a structural advantage that compounds as your reputation builds alongside the address. Meeting Clients Without Committing to a Full Lease Here's the thing about meeting room access: it's one of the more practical benefits people overlook when they think about virtual offices. Rather than taking clients to a café - which signals resource constraints about as clearly as a suburban home address does - you can book a boardroom in your CBD building for the hours you need it. Melbourne clients in professional services expect a proper meeting environment, particularly for early-stage conversations where trust is still being established. A well-appointed room with a city view, good coffee, and a professional reception team creates an experience a café simply can't replicate. And because you're only paying for the room when you use it, the cost per meeting is modest compared to what a full-time lease would run. For businesses that meet clients fortnightly or monthly rather than daily, this is a far more rational model than maintaining a permanent office that sits empty most of the week. You spend money on the moment that matters, not on floor space that doesn't. Conclusion A virtual office won't win clients on its own. But it clears away several of the small credibility barriers that stop good operators from being taken seriously in Melbourne's competitive market. A premium CBD address, professional call answering, and on-demand meeting rooms - taken together - put you in a position where your actual skills and offer do the heavy lifting, rather than your postcode. If you're asking whether a virtual office can help you win more Melbourne clients, the honest answer is yes, provided you choose a location and provider that genuinely reflects the standard your clients expect.

articles.title: AI Is Changing Mental Health Care
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Artificial intelligence is finding its way into mental health care, changing how people seek help, receive diagnoses, and connect with treatment providers. What once required a phone call or an office visit can now begin with a chatbot, an online questionnaire, or an automated screening tool. For people who have spent weeks trying to find a therapist, that sounds like progress. But the growing use of AI in mental health services is also raising concerns about patient safety, privacy, and the loss of human connection. Healthcare providers are under pressure to serve more patients while keeping costs down. Technology offers one answer. Yet researchers and mental health professionals are questioning whether faster services always mean better care. The issue is no longer simply whether AI belongs in mental healthcare. It's how much control these systems should have over decisions that affect people's lives. AI Is Making Mental Health Support Easier to Find Help Without the Long Wait One of AI's biggest advantages is accessibility. Many Americans face long waiting lists, high treatment costs, and a shortage of mental health professionals. Rural communities often have fewer providers, making regular appointments difficult. AI-powered tools are starting to fill some of those gaps. Chatbots can answer basic mental health questions, guide users through stress management exercises, and help identify symptoms that need professional attention. Some platforms also use automated questionnaires to connect patients with appropriate services. Research suggests these tools can offer meaningful support. A 2025 Dartmouth College clinical trial involving 210 adults found that participants using an AI therapy chatbot called Therabot experienced greater improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms than those in a comparison group. Researchers stressed that larger studies and continued clinical supervision remain necessary. The appeal is easy to understand. Someone struggling with anxiety at midnight doesn't have to wait until morning to find basic support. Technology also makes it easier to locate professional care. A search for mental health treatment Florida can bring up treatment resources within seconds. Still, finding a provider and receiving effective treatment are two different things. AI can help people identify available services, but it cannot guarantee that those services are affordable, appropriate, or accessible when patients need them. And that difference matters. When Technology Starts Making Healthcare Decisions The Problem With Automated Referrals AI becomes more controversial when it moves beyond providing information and begins influencing treatment decisions. Healthcare systems increasingly use digital screening tools to assess symptoms and determine where patients should receive care. These systems can process large amounts of information quickly. They also reduce administrative work. But mental health conditions rarely fit neatly into a questionnaire. A patient experiencing depression might describe feeling tired rather than hopeless. Someone dealing with trauma might struggle to explain their symptoms. Others may minimize their condition because they fear judgment. A computer can record their answers. Understanding what those answers leave out is harder. The debate has already reached California. In July 2026, CalMatters reported that the National Union of Healthcare Workers had filed a complaint accusing Kaiser Permanente of using an automated system to screen mental health patients without proper clinician oversight. Kaiser disputed the allegations, saying its online screening tool does not use AI to diagnose patients or make clinical decisions. The company maintained that licensed professionals remain responsible for clinical judgments. California regulators were investigating the complaint. The dispute reflects a larger concern about who controls access to mental health services. Patients dealing with several conditions at once face particular challenges. Someone seeking dual diagnosis treatment Bend Oregon , for example, may need care that addresses both mental health symptoms and substance use disorders. These conditions often affect each other. A screening system that evaluates them separately can miss important connections. Automated referrals can help organize services, but they also risk becoming another barrier when patients cannot easily challenge a decision or speak with a qualified professional. Can AI Really Understand Emotional Distress? When a Friendly Response Gets It Wrong AI chatbots are designed to communicate naturally. They can respond with comforting language, ask follow-up questions, and maintain conversations that feel personal. For some users, that makes discussing difficult emotions less intimidating. However, sounding understanding isn't the same as understanding. A 2025 Stanford University study found that AI therapy chatbots sometimes reinforced stigma toward people experiencing conditions such as schizophrenia and alcohol dependence. Researchers also identified cases where chatbots responded poorly to statements involving suicidal thoughts or delusions, raising concerns about their ability to recognize serious warning signs. The findings exposed a weakness in automated emotional support. AI systems learn patterns from large amounts of data, but human emotions don't always follow predictable patterns. Someone discussing addiction may be expressing fear, shame, or a desire to change. A chatbot can identify certain words without fully understanding the circumstances behind them. This becomes especially important for people entering addiction treatment. A search for rehab center Deerfield Beach may help someone locate treatment services, but recovery involves more than identifying a facility. Patients often need professional assessments, ongoing emotional support, and care that reflects their personal experiences. AI can help organize information about these needs. It cannot replace the trust that develops between a patient and a trained clinician. Researchers are also questioning how chatbot safety is measured. In July 2026, Stanford researchers reported significant disagreements among psychiatrists evaluating the safety of AI-generated mental health responses. Their findings suggest that even expert assessments can differ when emotional situations become complex. That raises a difficult question. If professionals sometimes disagree about the safest response, how much responsibility should an automated system carry? The Privacy and Fairness Questions Are Growing Who Benefits From Healthcare Automation? Mental health information is deeply personal. Patients may disclose experiences involving trauma, addiction, family conflict, or thoughts they have never shared with anyone else. As AI becomes part of healthcare, more of that information passes through digital systems. This raises questions about where patient data is stored, who can access it, and whether it can be used to train future technology. The World Health Organization has emphasized that healthcare AI needs strong data protections, transparent systems, and safeguards against discrimination. Without those protections, technology risks worsening inequalities that already affect healthcare access. These concerns are particularly important for low-income patients, older adults, people with disabilities, and communities with limited internet access. A digital-first healthcare system assumes everyone has reliable technology and feels comfortable using it. That isn't always true. People who struggle with online forms or automated phone systems can find themselves further removed from the professionals they are trying to reach. There are also concerns about how AI systems influence decisions about treatment intensity. Someone considering residential mental health treatment California needs a careful assessment of symptoms, safety, medical history, and personal circumstances. Such decisions should involve qualified professionals who can examine the complete picture rather than relying solely on automated scores. Regulators are beginning to address these challenges. In August 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration sought public feedback on how generative AI medical devices should be evaluated and monitored, including questions about safety and risks after products reach the market. The growing attention reflects how quickly healthcare technology is changing. Yet regulation alone cannot solve every problem. A system may meet technical standards while still leaving patients confused about their treatment options or unable to reach someone who can explain a decision. The Future of Mental Health Care Still Needs People AI has a place in mental healthcare. Research shows encouraging results for certain tools, and automation can reduce paperwork, improve access to information, and help providers manage growing patient demand. But these benefits should not come at the expense of human care. The greatest risk is that healthcare organizations begin treating faster processing as proof of better outcomes. A completed questionnaire isn't a clinical assessment. An automated referral isn't a treatment plan. And a chatbot offering reassuring words isn't necessarily providing safe mental health support. For underserved communities, the stakes are even higher. People who already struggle with healthcare costs, insurance restrictions, and provider shortages have the most to lose when automated systems create new barriers. The challenge facing healthcare providers and policymakers is making sure technology supports clinical judgment rather than replacing it. Mental health treatment depends on trust, communication, and the ability to recognize when someone needs more than a standard response. AI can help people reach that care. But the person on the other side of the screen still needs to be heard.

articles.title: Livorno Dockworkers Are Trying to Block the Weapons of War
articles.author: Alex Colston
articles.content: Livorno, Italy — “Sunaid X, Sunaid X, Sunaid X, this is Sumud, do you copy?” “You’re calling Sunaid X.” “Sunaid X, you are carrying supplies to a military base that is deeply involved in Zionists’ warfare and the genocide of the Palestinian people. The port is blocked for you. You’re not welcome here.” So went last Thursday’s radio exchange between Global Sumud Flotilla (GSF) activist Luca Poggi and the bridge of the Sunaid X, a container ship that local unions had identified as a supplier of the NATO military base Sigonella, the US Navy’s air station in Sicily. After lying in wait for a week, living aboard three GSF sailboats at the port, around ten GSF members sprang into action midday on October 22. A Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat faces a Guardia di Finanza patrol boat at the mouth of Livorno’s harbor. Top right: the Sunaid X on the horizon off the Tuscan coast. Bottom right: containers stacked behind a wall at the Port of Livorno. October 22, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto) According to a statement from Gruppo Autonomo Portuali (GAP), an autonomous collective of Livorno dockworkers, and the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), an independent rank-and-file union that has led Livorno’s port blockades, the Sunaid X links Livorno with Sigonella for the US Defense Logistics Agency. The shipping vessel was due to load bulk chemicals, paints, food, and lithium batteries for drones at the Terminal Darsena Toscana (TDT). Weather delays had already pushed back the Sunaid X’s arrival by two days . The ship missed its 2 p.m. Thursday berth at the TDT, Livorno’s main container terminal. Two of the sailboats held the harbor entrance, while the third took up position at the ship’s berth, and from roughly 2:30 to 8:30 p.m., the Sunaid X lay at anchor offshore. On land, USB called a strike, and GAP and USB picketed the terminal gate. When the ship finally docked that evening, dockworkers on the night shift refused to service it, and Friday’s morning shift did the same. The Guardia di Finanza, Italy’s militarized financial and customs police, seized the three sailboats and held the GSF crews into the evening at a barracks beside the harbor master’s office. All ten were released late Thursday after being reported to prosecutors for “disruption of a public service,” an accusation that will go before a local judge, where the defendants will be represented by Tatiana Montella, a lawyer who works with GSF, according to the organization. The boats remain confiscated and under seizure. A solidarity rally had gathered in the city that evening as the GSF activists were detained. “The boats of the Global Sumud Flotilla have led the way, and dockworkers have continued this fight on the docks, transforming solidarity into concrete action,” one protester told the local press . “Words are no longer enough: we must stop the trafficking that fuels war!” Guardia di Finanza officers seen from inside the cabin of a Global Sumud Flotilla sailboat in Livorno’s harbor on October 22, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto) The dockworkers suspended their strike after winning a meeting with Livorno’s Prefecture, TDT, the Port Authority, and the harbor master. USB has said that four “suspicious” containers waiting to be loaded onto Sunaid X held drone batteries, military equipment, gas, and propellants, a claim that has not been independently verified. According to the striking dockworkers, the Port Authority agreed to inspect the cargo, but it is unconfirmed whether the inspection took place or what it found. The Sunaid X has since left for Augusta, in Sicily, where it was again met by GSF activists at sea on Monday . The Latest Action of a Yearlong Effort Thursday’s joint GSF-USB-GAP action is the latest in a year of escalating attempts by Livorno’s dockworkers to stop war cargo from moving through their port. It was also the first time GSF boats and striking dockworkers moved together against the same vessel. “You have to pick the important cases,” said Giovanni Ceraolo, who has organized with USB since 2014 and now works on its national ports coordination. “You have to understand what the right moment is and the right situation, because if you think you can block everything, in the end, you block nothing.” Ceraolo sat down with me for an hour-long interview, conducted through an interpreter, on October 20, the day the Sunaid X was first due in port. “Weapons pass through the ports every day,” he said, “and it would be practically impossible to think you could block every shipment.” Livorno’s harbor master’s office reported that more than six hundred tons of explosives, mostly ammunition and rocket motors, were shipped from the port to countries outside the European Union between January 2025 and May 2026, though the data , obtained by the journalist Linda Maggiori and port safety representatives, do not show where any of it ended up. Law 185 of 1990 bars Italy from exporting arms to countries at war or under embargo and from letting them pass through its ports. The law is “almost never enforced,” Ceraolo said, but he noted that filing a formal complaint, “together with the action, the strike,” has at times been enough to call a shipment into question. Enforcing it has become a standing demand of the port strikes, and it was a plank of the national port strike that USB and ORSA Porti called in May. Still, Ceraolo was clear that it would not matter if the shipments were judged legal under the law. “Even if there were military traffic authorized under this law, we’d be against it anyway, and we’d act anyway,” he said. “Weapons are weapons, period.” USB and GAP have developed a three-pronged method, to which GSF has now added a blockade by sea: “Information, pickets, strike. That’s the only method we have for now, and it’s working, on and off.” The information comes mostly from the dockworkers. When activists blocked a military train at Pisa in March , Ceraolo said, the tip came from workers at the Piombino steelworks, where the train was being loaded. Next, the picket and the strike play out on the ground. “In practice, there are only two ways to block this traffic: with pickets and blockades, and with the strike. When we’ve managed to do both, we’ve pulled it off.” Put a physical blockade together with a strike in the rail and port sectors that have to handle the cargo, he said, and “you put war logistics in serious difficulty.” He traces the method back to September 2025. As the fall Global Sumud Flotilla sailed toward Gaza, protesters forced open one of the port’s gates and occupied the quay where the SLNC Severn, a US-flagged ship serving the nearby US Army base at Camp Darby , was due to berth. “We stayed there three days straight, twenty-four hours a day,” Ceraolo said. “All together: students, workers, dockworkers, teachers, the whole city. Even the mayor came.” The ship never docked . “For us, it was an important event,” he said, because of how close Livorno is to “one of the biggest American bases in Europe.” A week later, the Israeli-owned ZIM Virginia docked and left the same evening without loading or unloading any cargo, after dockworkers struck at the call of Filt-CGIL, the transport federation of Italy’s largest national union confederation. When Israel intercepted the flotilla in October 2025, Livorno joined the general strike that shut down ports and highways and disrupted rail lines across Italy . Even the organizers were unprepared for the national reverberations of the call to action. “What happened last year was something nobody in Italy expected, and least of all us in Livorno,” Ceraolo said. “We were flooded with phone calls from people asking how to go on strike, because these were people who had never been on strike in their lives. They didn’t even know what striking meant.” People “who, the day before, never even thought about it were, the next day, behind a burning barricade on the Aurelia ,” the coastal highway, he said. “Ordinary people.” The lesson Ceraolo took was that mass moments can’t be summoned on command. “There’s nothing automatic between daily work and mass moments,” he said. “You have to try, you have to push, talk to people.” What September and October proved, he said, is “that if the conditions are there, people will take to the streets.” Left: a poster for the October 30 general strike on a door in Livorno. Right: Giovanni Ceraolo of the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB). October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto) On October 30, international dockworkers, seafarers, and port workers plan to test that idea well beyond Livorno. The day of action grew out of a declaration agreed on by Mediterranean and European port unions in Istanbul in May. In July, it was announced by unions in six countries : France, Greece, the Basque Country, Turkey, Morocco, and Italy, where USB and ORSA Porti signed on. Organizers now say about one hundred ports in seventeen countries will take part, among them dockworkers in Oakland, Hamburg, and Veracruz, and that around forty thousand containers could be held up for the day. In Italy, eight ports are set to strike, Livorno and Genoa among them, and USB has called a general strike across every sector. The sectoral demands go beyond the genocide in Gaza. Organizers are calling for an end to using ports to move arms to war zones or as bases for NATO, the US, or EU militaries; an end to European rearmament; and higher wages for the workers who keep the ports running. The strike has been endorsed by seventeen Palestinian trade union bodies. Disturbing the Machine From the Inside “I have a son, who is what drives me to do what I do,” said Simone D’Aversa, a thirty-nine-year-old Livorno dockworker who helped found GAP. Over the past few years, he said, he came to see his own work as “extremely involved in war,” and it pushed him to act. “It made me commit: to try to find a way to become something that disturbs this machine from the inside.” Italy’s labor movement has two tiers. The big national confederations — the Italian General Confederation of Labor (CGIL), the Italian Confederation of Trades Unions (CISL), and the Italian Labour Union (UIL), known in Italian as the confederali — negotiate the national contracts that set most workers’ pay. Smaller, independent sindacati di base , or rank-and-file unions such as USB, have built their membership on the shop floor. When GAP started out, D’Aversa said, the group went to every union in the port and asked them to protect any worker who refused to handle certain cargo. “On one side, we found USB willing,” he said. “It’s a rank-and-file union that had already been working against the arms trade for years. On the other side, we hit a wall” with the union confederations. GAP’s members now range from USB members to workers without a union. Some still belong to the big unions, he said, and these workers are unhappy with them but can’t break away “for reasons that are also purely about their jobs.” He described GAP and USB as two “gears” that are “separate and autonomous from each other. In practice, when it’s needed for blockades and strikes, they act as a single entity.” The organized dockworkers can’t do it alone, D’Aversa said. GAP works with what he called “a strong city network” of student collectives, social centers, associations, and environmental groups. “There’s a real diversity of struggles, and that’s partly what lets us make up for the fact that, yes, we represent Livorno’s dockworkers, but not all of Livorno’s dockworkers,” he said. “So we need a push that also comes from the territory and from the city, which is starting to feel that the port [is] something collective.” He sees that push as an expression of larger possibilities. In Italy, he said, there is “a total lack of trust in politics, in institutional politics, and instead a huge need among people to feel part of politics.” Left: cranes at the Port of Livorno. Right: Simone D’Aversa, a Livorno dockworker who helped found the Gruppo Autonomo Portuali. October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto) Last fall’s mobilizations, he said, “came from a union’s leadership, yes, but just as much from the push the masses gave [for] the union to move.” What gave that push a direction was a speech in Genoa by Riccardo Rudino of CALP, Genoa’s autonomous dockworkers’ collective, who promised that, if the flotilla was stopped, the ports would block everything. “Having a date and a clear goal was the spark that made all the mobilizations possible.” “It’s true that governments are complicit in what happened,” D’Aversa said. “But I think the act that most challenges our privilege is admitting that we are complicit with our governments, if we don’t do [on October 30] what we did in September and October.” For Luca Poggi, a twenty-nine-year-old former economist at an environmental nongovernmental organization (NGO), who quit his job after the flotilla’s second mission to organize full-time with GSF, the boats are the seafaring half of the same confrontation at the port. “The disruption of the supply chain is what can hit the genocide the most,” he said, “because you hit on the economics.” The people GSF is up against, he said, “are CEOs of big banks, big investment funds . . . prime ministers of important governments. So, we are fighting against the most powerful people and the most powerful entities in the world.” GSF, he stressed, does not break the supply chain itself. “We don’t go and assault vessels. We are nonviolent.” He emphasized that the point is numbers. “They might be a hundred. We will be one million,” he said. “The moment we are one million, even money loses its value.” The boats have become a symbol of “David against Goliath . . . we load toys, baby formula, food, medicines, and we go against those who load bullets.” The sea gives GSF room to maneuver that acting on land does not. “It’s much easier to act at sea than acting on land,” he said. “The sea doesn’t have the same law of the land.” Luca Poggi of the Global Sumud Flotilla aboard a sailboat in Livorno’s harbor, with a handheld radio. October 20, 2026. (Andrea Bellaroto) Two days before Thursday’s blockade, Poggi called it GSF’s “way to launch the strike of the 30th of October, Flotilla-style.” The goal was to “show the participation of this company in the war and in the genocide, and also the complicity of our governments that allow all this to happen.” Each sailboat would take a role at a different stage of the ship’s maneuvering, and planning for the action was conducted in person on the boats while awaiting the arrival of Sunaid X. “Consider that the ship we want to block is eight thousand tons, while our boats are less than eight,” he said. “We will not do anything dangerous. We will stay far. But at the same time, we have ways to block it from entering the port.” “If a ship is delayed by one day, the delays pile up, and a logistics mechanism breaks,” Ceraolo said. “It’s a political signal but also economic damage. Both things together. So, for us, beyond everything, it’s a historic day.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
