articles.title: Busy Morning
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Mornings rarely go exactly as planned. Sometimes there is barely enough time to choose an outfit, prepare breakfast, and get ready for the day, let alone create an attractive hairstyle. For anyone who wants beautiful hair without a complicated morning routine, OQ Hair Headband Wigs offer an interesting styling option. These wigs combine convenience with versatility, helping you explore different looks while keeping your preparation simple. A headband wig features a wig cap with a fabric band positioned at the front. Unlike many traditional lace wigs, this design does not require lace trimming or adhesive application in the same way. The headband covers the front edge, creating a straightforward way to wear a finished hairstyle. Depending on the design, adjustable straps and combs may help keep the wig in place. Discover the Convenience of Headband Wigs One of the most appealing aspects of a headband wig is its simple design. People who find traditional wig installation time-consuming may appreciate having another option that requires fewer preparation steps. Once the wig is positioned correctly, the headband can be adjusted, and the hair can be arranged according to personal preference. OQ Hair Headband Wigs come in different hair textures and styles, allowing wearers to choose an appearance that complements their daily activities. Depending on the particular model, options may include straight hair, flowing waves, deep waves, or defined curls. Another advantage is the opportunity to experiment with accessories. A basic headband creates a clean appearance, while a patterned band or decorative scarf can introduce a different mood. This flexibility makes headband wigs suitable for people who enjoy changing their hairstyles without completely changing their hairpieces. Five Quick Hairstyles to Try Before Leaving Home 1. The Effortless Everyday Style When you are running late, a simple hairstyle can be the perfect solution. Position your headband wig comfortably, secure the fastening system, and gently arrange the hair around your face. Depending on its texture, you can use your fingers or a suitable brush to smooth the lengths. This look works well for grocery shopping, university classes, casual meetings, and everyday errands. Pair it with comfortable clothing and minimal accessories for a relaxed appearance that still feels put together. 2. Polished Waves for Work A wavy headband wig can add movement and softness to a professional outfit. Choose a texture that suits your preference, then gently separate the waves to create a balanced finish. Avoid excessive brushing if you want to preserve the original wave pattern. You can complement this hairstyle with a tailored jacket, a neutral blouse, or a simple dress. A solid-colored headband helps maintain a professional appearance without making the overall look feel too formal. The best part is that you can achieve an attractive result without spending your entire morning using multiple styling tools. 3. A Ponytail for a Busy Schedule Some mornings call for a hairstyle that keeps hair away from your face. Depending on the cap construction and flexibility of your selected headband wig, a ponytail may be a convenient choice. Gather the hair gently and secure it at a comfortable height. Avoid pulling the wig too tightly or placing unnecessary tension on its cap. Before choosing this style, check whether the particular model supports ponytail styling. This practical look can be useful for commuting, travelling, exercising lightly, or completing everyday tasks. 4. Natural-Looking Curls with Added Character Curly textures can bring personality to an outfit without requiring an elaborate styling routine. A kinky curly or deep wave headband wig may be a suitable option for anyone who enjoys textured hairstyles. Start by gently separating the curls with your fingers. If necessary, use a small amount of suitable hair moisturizer or leave-in conditioner, following the product's care instructions. Let the curls settle naturally rather than repeatedly brushing them. For an attractive finishing touch, choose a headband that complements the hair color. The result can feel expressive and stylish while remaining easy to manage. 5. A Fresh Look with a Decorative Headband You do not always need a different wig to create a different appearance. Sometimes, changing the accessory is enough. Try a soft neutral headband for everyday wear, a printed scarf for a casual outing, or a coordinated color for an event. You can also match the accessory with your clothing or handbag to create a more consistent outfit. Before adding a separate accessory, make sure it does not interfere with the wig's original fastening system. Comfort and a secure fit should always come first. Choosing the Right OQ Hair Headband Wig Finding the right headband wig begins with understanding your styling preferences. Consider whether you prefer straight strands, loose waves, defined curls, or a fuller textured appearance. Think about the length you feel comfortable managing and whether you want a style suitable for everyday use or occasional special events. Hair composition is another important consideration. Some headband wigs are made from human hair, while other products may use synthetic fibers. Read the individual product description carefully to confirm the materials, available colors, lengths, density, and recommended styling methods. You should also consider cap size and adjustability. A wig that fits comfortably is easier to wear throughout the day. Follow the manufacturer's measuring instructions, and check the fastening features before purchasing. Finally, choose a style that works with your lifestyle rather than selecting one based solely on appearance. A practical hairstyle should fit your routine, maintenance preferences, and personal sense of style. Keeping Your Headband Wig Beautiful Regular maintenance helps preserve the appearance and usability of a headband wig. Begin by detangling gently before washing, working from the ends toward the roots. Use products appropriate for the hair material and follow the manufacturer's washing instructions. For curly textures, finger-detangling or using a wide-tooth comb may help minimize disruption to the curl pattern. For straighter styles, a suitable brush can help manage tangles. When using heat on a human hair wig, apply heat protection and avoid unnecessarily high temperatures. Synthetic wigs require particular attention to heat limitations. Allow the wig to dry thoroughly before storing it. Keep it in a clean, dry place, ideally on a suitable wig stand or in protective storage. The fabric headband also deserves attention because sweat, makeup, and styling products can accumulate on it over time. A consistent care routine can help keep your wig looking presentable and make future styling sessions easier. Final Thoughts Getting ready in the morning does not have to involve a lengthy hairstyle routine. With the right headband wig, you can explore different textures, experiment with accessories, and find an appearance that suits your plans without making hair preparation unnecessarily complicated. OQ Hair headband wig and glueless wig provide a versatile option for people who appreciate convenient styling and the freedom to change their look. Whether you prefer relaxed waves, defined curls, or a simple everyday hairstyle, the key is choosing a design that complements your preferences and feels comfortable to wear. Instead of treating hairstyling as another stressful morning responsibility, make it an easy part of expressing your personality. Select a suitable wig, care for it properly, and keep a few favorite headbands ready for different occasions. With a little preparation, you can start your day feeling organized, confident, and ready for whatever comes next.

articles.title: Roof Repair Protects Your Home
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Your roof rarely gets much attention until something goes wrong. One missing shingle can seem harmless, then a hard rain turns your ceiling into a warning sign. If you own a home, understanding roof repair helps you avoid bigger costs, protect resale value, and keep your place structurally sound. In a city like Atlanta, where heat, storms, humidity, and heavy tree cover all show up in the same year, roof problems can escalate faster than most people expect. How timely repair saves you money in the long run Roof repair is usually far cheaper than replacing a full roofing system or fixing interior water damage. The math gets ugly fast when a minor issue spreads into rotten decking, mold remediation, damaged drywall, and electrical work. Think about a small flashing failure around a vent pipe. Fixing it early may involve a targeted repair and a routine inspection. Ignore it for a year, and you could be paying for soaked insulation, stained ceilings, and compromised wood framing. If you are comparing options for professional service, an experienced Atlanta roof repair company can identify whether you need a simple fix, storm-related repair, or broader structural attention. That kind of diagnosis matters because not every leak calls for a full replacement, despite what panic might suggest. Why roof damage tends to sneak up on you Roof issues often start small and stay quiet for months. A lifted shingle, cracked flashing, or clogged valley may not cause an obvious leak right away. Water can move behind materials, soak decking, and weaken insulation before you spot a single stain indoors. Atlanta homes deal with a rough mix of weather stress. Summer heat can age shingles faster. Thunderstorms can rip off tabs or drive rain into weak seams. Falling branches are another common headache, especially in neighborhoods with mature trees. You might think the roof is fine because it looks okay from the street. Roofs are good at hiding problems until repair turns urgent. That delay is where budgets start taking damage too. Warning signs you should never brush off A roof rarely fails without leaving clues. The problem is that many homeowners miss them or assume they can wait until next season. Roofs, unfortunately, do not care about your calendar. Watch for these signs: - Water stains on ceilings or upper walls - Curling, cracked, or missing shingles - Dark streaks or patches that hold moisture - Granules collecting in gutters - Sagging spots along the roofline - Flashing that looks loose around chimneys or vents - Higher indoor humidity or musty attic smells A sudden spike in energy bills can also point to roof trouble. When moisture gets into roofing layers or attic insulation, your HVAC system has to work harder. It is not exactly the kind of home upgrade anyone wants. The connection between roof condition and home value Your roof has a direct effect on how buyers, appraisers, and insurers view your property. Even if you are not planning to sell soon, deferred maintenance tends to show up in your home’s marketability. A damaged roof can: - Lower curb appeal immediately - Raise concerns during buyer inspections - Lead to insurance complications or higher premiums - Trigger demands for repair credits during a sale - Make the whole home seem less maintained Buyers notice visible wear fast. They may not understand flashing details or ventilation ratios, but they definitely understand stains, patchy shingles, and sagging lines. Those signals make people wonder what else has been ignored. A solid repair history, on the other hand, shows responsibility. It tells future buyers the home has been cared for instead of patched together with crossed fingers. What a professional roof repair visit should include A proper roof repair appointment should involve more than someone pointing at a leak and giving you a number. You want a careful evaluation of the roofing system, not a guess in work boots. A strong inspection usually covers: - Shingle condition and attachment - Flashing around penetrations and edges - Signs of storm or wind damage - Soft spots in decking - Gutter drainage issues - Attic ventilation and moisture conditions - Evidence of prior patch jobs that may fail again The goal is to find both the symptom and the source. Water often enters in one area and appears somewhere else indoors, which makes DIY diagnosis unreliable. A repair that only covers the visible leak can miss the actual failure point. Then you get to pay twice, which is a terrible tradition. Why Atlanta homes need location-specific roofing attention Not every roofing issue plays out the same way in every city. Atlanta presents a specific set of challenges tied to climate, vegetation, and seasonal storm patterns. Local knowledge matters more than many homeowners realize. Frequent humidity can encourage algae growth and moisture retention. Intense sun exposure can age roofing materials unevenly. Heavy rainstorms test drainage fast, especially on older homes with worn flashing or clogged gutters. Tree-heavy lots also create special risks. Branch impact is the obvious one, but shade and debris can be just as damaging over time. Wet leaves trap moisture, and that moisture can shorten the life of roofing materials. A contractor who understands Atlanta-area roof behavior is better equipped to spot patterns that may be common locally but easy to miss in a generic inspection approach. Smart ways to reduce future roof repair problems You cannot control the weather, but you can make roof problems less likely. Consistent maintenance gives you a better shot at catching issues before they become expensive and disruptive. Here are practical steps that help: - Schedule inspections after major storms - Clean gutters so water can drain properly - Trim overhanging branches near the roof surface - Check the attic for damp insulation or musty odors - Look for shingle debris around downspouts - Address small leaks immediately, even if they seem minor - Keep records of repairs and inspections It also helps to walk your property after severe weather. You do not need to climb onto the roof. Just look for shingles on the ground, bent gutters, or visible impact damage. The best roof repair strategy is not dramatic. It is consistent, informed, and a little boring. Boring is good when the ceiling stays dry. Final thoughts on protecting your home before small issues grow Roof repair sits in that category of home maintenance people tend to postpone until the problem becomes impossible to ignore. By then, the damage usually has a head start. If you pay attention to early warning signs, act quickly after storms, and bring in qualified professionals when something looks off, you give yourself better odds of avoiding major structural and financial stress. You also protect your home’s value in a very practical way. A healthy roof does more than keep rain out. It supports energy efficiency, preserves interior materials, strengthens resale potential, and adds peace of mind. That is a strong return for taking the top of your house seriously before it starts making decisions for you.

articles.title: Beyond the Makeover
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A renovation can make a house look impressive without making it more valuable. Finishes attract attention, but buyers also notice awkward layouts and neglected maintenance. The challenge is choosing improvements that support daily living and lasting future value. Consider the property, likely buyers, and surrounding market. Spending wisely takes careful thought. Fix What Buyers Would Worry About First A polished interior cannot distract everyone from peeling exterior finishes, recurring leaks, or windows that barely open. These issues raise questions about what else has been neglected. Before choosing decorative upgrades, inspect the roof, siding, drainage, and visible signs of water damage. Ask whether a problem needs a targeted repair or a larger replacement. For exterior work, a contractor such as KVN Construction offers siding, roofing, window, door, gutter, and painting services. Those improvements can address weather protection and appearance together, provided the scope responds to actual problems. Ask about inspection findings, materials, installation details, and warranties before committing. A fresh exterior is most persuasive when the underlying work is sound. Know the Difference Between Cost and Value A project costing twenty thousand dollars does not automatically add twenty thousand dollars to an appraisal. Buyers compare a property with available alternatives, not with the owner's receipts. A beautifully renovated room can improve marketability without recovering its entire cost. Separate three kinds of benefit. Some projects prevent expensive deterioration. Others make rooms more comfortable or convenient. A smaller group may influence what a buyer is willing to pay. These categories overlap, but they are not identical. Start by asking what the property lacks rather than what would look exciting in a photograph. Replacing a leaking roof may be more urgent than installing designer cabinets, even if the cabinets are easier to show off. Keep the Design Consistent With the Property An extravagant renovation can feel strangely out of place when everything around it remains ordinary. Imported stone, complicated lighting, and custom fittings may suit some homes, but they are difficult to justify solely as resale investments. Look at the finishes and features buyers tend to encounter in comparable properties. Notice overall condition, usable storage, kitchen functionality, and how rooms connect. The aim is not to imitate another listing. It is to avoid improvements that create an expensive mismatch. Consistency also matters within the house. One spectacular bathroom beside several visibly neglected spaces may highlight the unfinished work. Sometimes modest upgrades across multiple rooms create a more convincing impression than a lavish transformation in one corner. Give Hidden Problems a Place in the Budget Demolition has a talent for revealing inconvenient surprises. Old plumbing, damaged framing, moisture behind finishes, or unsafe electrical work can change the cost and schedule before the exciting part begins. Ignoring that possibility does not make it disappear. The guidance on controlling household moisture explains why correcting leaks, drainage problems, and damp conditions matters. Concealing damage beneath new materials can leave buyers with the same problem in a prettier package. Build a contingency into the budget, especially when opening walls or floors. Agree on how unexpected findings will be documented and approved. That conversation is much easier before a contractor is standing beside an exposed pipe waiting for an answer. Spend on Function Before Flashy Extras A renovation should improve how a property works. A kitchen with adequate preparation space, dependable appliances, and sensible lighting often feels better than one dominated by an expensive statement feature. The same principle applies to bathrooms, storage, entrances, and utility areas. Walk through the home as someone unfamiliar with it. Are doors awkward to open? Is there enough light for everyday tasks? Can furniture fit without blocking circulation? Does the layout create needless obstacles? Solutions need not involve knocking down walls. Better storage, repaired hardware, thoughtful lighting, and durable surfaces can make a meaningful difference. Prioritize changes that remove genuine frustrations, then decide whether decorative extras still fit the budget. Hire Carefully and Compare the Entire Scope A low estimate can become costly when important work is excluded. Before choosing a contractor, request written descriptions of materials, preparation, labor, cleanup, expected timing, and procedures for changes. Clarify responsibility for permits and inspections where applicable. The advice on avoiding home improvement scams highlights the importance of checking credentials, comparing written estimates, and reviewing contracts before paying. These precautions protect more than the project budget; they help preserve a record of work for future buyers. Ask questions when quotes differ significantly. One contractor may include repairs or waterproofing that another leaves unspecified. Comparing only the final price can mean comparing entirely different projects. Plan the Work Around Your Selling Timeline Timing changes the calculation. A homeowner planning to stay for years may value comfort and durability more than immediate resale returns. Someone preparing to list soon needs to consider whether construction delays, financing costs, and disruption are justified. Schedule necessary repairs before cosmetic work so finished surfaces are not damaged twice. Confirm delivery timelines for important materials and leave time for final inspections and corrections. Rushing an unfinished project onto the market can create more concern than a carefully maintained, less fashionable interior. Sometimes cleaning, repairing obvious defects, and improving lighting will be enough. Renovation should answer a specific need, not become an automatic step before every sale. Let the Finished Work Speak for Itself Good renovations make a home easier to understand and trust. Doors close properly. Materials feel consistent. Water stays where it belongs. Rooms work without making occupants invent awkward routines. Keep permits, warranties, invoices, and photographs of concealed work when available. They help explain what changed and may support questions during a sale. Avoid promising buyers that an upgrade guarantees higher appraisal value or lower bills; those outcomes depend on many factors. The smartest investment is rarely the most dramatic one. It is a deliberate improvement that solves a real problem, suits the property, and holds up after the excitement of construction fades.

articles.title: Members Alarmed by End-Run around Democracy at Buffalo Health Care Local
articles.author: Sarah Hughes
articles.content: Things had been tense for some time inside the leadership of Communications Workers (CWA) Local 1168, a 4,800-member health care union based near Buffalo, New York. Still, it was a high-functioning local with a busy calendar of events, stewards handling grievances, organizers pursuing leads, and leaders organizing at work. So it was a surprise to members in June when their parent union, CWA, put the local into trusteeship, at the request of the local’s president and seven of the nineteen executive board members. Trusteeship meant the union’s bylaws and elected leaders were suspended, and most of its work temporarily ground to a halt. The appointed Director of Organizing and Mobilizing Mary Nowocien and elected Vice President Patrick Weisansal II found themselves locked out of their group chats, email, and union hall, and facing an internal union prosecution. A staffer of CWA District 1, Erin Spaulding, was assigned as trustee—tasked with maintaining the functioning of the local, setting up and overseeing judicial processes for the charges against officers, and making a plan to return the union to local control. Nowocien and Weisansal saw the sudden trusteeship as an escalation of a long-running conflict and a deliberate undermining of the upcoming union elections. Weisansal had just announced his intention to run against incumbent President Cori Gambini. Now the elections are on hold until the trials are over, whenever that is. And lately, the employer has been taking advantage of the turmoil in the union. While the allegations are serious, members are concerned that the trusteeship was a nuclear option for an internal financial matter and that it has torn apart relationships at the local, weakened opposition to management’s schemes and denied democratic processes to an active, engaged union membership. ALLEGED TIMECARD ISSUES The trusteeship filing lists the cause as “serious allegations of financial misconduct” from officers and “dueling charges” between leaders. Gambini and Executive Vice President Robert Andruszko had accused Nowocien and Weisansal of defrauding the local of thousands of dollars, by getting paid by both the union and their employer for the same hours worked, and by falsifying records. These issues came to light during a timecard audit in the fall of 2025 by their employer, Kaleida Health. Nowocien and Weisansal acknowledged there were significant errors on old timecards and paychecks, but said it was the product of the employer’s faulty timekeeping and payroll system, and human error. The majority of other officers also had issues, they pointed out, but only some were being singled out for discipline by the local and the employer. Spaulding, the trustee, interviewed all the suspended officers and allowed the majority to return to their paid positions—with the exception of Nowocien, Weisansal, and three others not facing any charges: the Communications and Political Directors and one of the Area Vice Presidents. Also fired were two longtime staff organizers, on the grounds that there was no work for them to do, according to one, Ann Converso, who had recently helped organize a new unit of substance use disorder counselors and was gearing up for their first contract fight. Many current leaders on both sides of this schism were part of a reform caucus in Local 1168, the Caucus of Rank-and-File Healthcare Employees (CORHE), which dissolved when they won their positions in 2020. Since winning, Gambini and a few others have butted heads with Weisansal, Nowocien, and others over how to tackle problems. The latter camp frequently organized their facility—Buffalo General Hospital, the union’s largest unit—to push back against management’s changes and violations. Gambini and leaders aligned with her argued that that wasn’t the right approach—that they had to pick their fights and not overextend the membership, according to Weisansal. One Buffalo General steward, who asked to not be named, said members were appalled that the trustee had removed elected officers. “If our employer treated one of our members in a similar fashion,” the steward said, “union leadership would rally around them and fight to return them to their position!” Spaulding wrote in a public FAQ posted on the local’s social media that the temporary administration “is not intended to be punitive or find guilt against any individual in the Local. It is intended to stabilize the Local while issues are investigated and resolved.” She also wrote that staffing decisions were made based on “operational needs of the local, nature of pending charges, and interviews conducted with each board member [by the trustee].” CWA, Spaulding, and Gambini did not respond to requests for comment. Re-instated Area Vice President Kim Kornowski emailed Labor Notes , writing, “we are a democratic union that includes our members in all aspects of our work. In 2020, we ran together on the C.O.R.H.E. slate and implemented our platform. A few board members engaged in serious financial misconduct, and we requested that the local be placed under trusteeship while these issues are addressed.” A THOUSAND SIGNATURES Some of the former members of CORHE re-formed as a committee and started reaching out to members. They drafted a petition to the trustee, asking for a general membership meeting, an end to the trusteeship, a neutral election to be held this fall, and for the elected officers to be returned to their positions in the meantime. In the local’s bylaws, if 20 percent of the members (around 1000 people) request a meeting, leadership is compelled to hold one. The members of the reorganized CORHE worked to get the petition signed: they printed paper copies, talked to co-workers, and asked colleagues in different units to gather signatures. Weisansal said he appealed to people’s commitment to union democracy. “The in-person membership meeting we were supposed to have got canceled,” he said. “There’s been a lot of anger about the [virtual] town hall calls, [because] they filter the questions. People aren’t stupid, and they're angry. “What has been helpful is not asking people to be the judge or jury,” he said. “What we’re asking is, do you believe in democracy, and if members should be able to make decisions about their own union.” Nowocien and Weisensal are well-known union activists, so many members were eager to sign on in their defense. “There are still a lot of good people in this union that see how wrong this is all going,” said Ashley Emminger, a mobilizer at Buffalo General. “They just want this [trusteeship] to end, to have the people we elected back where they belong, and elections move forward.” Weisansal and Nowocien have had to fight for their positions before. In 2019 they were removed from the Local 1168 board by a previous leadership, they say in retaliation for their organizing. (Gambini was not present for that vote, and fought for them to be reinstated.) At that time, they gathered the signatures to compel a membership meeting, 200 people showed up to support them, and the two were returned to their positions. The following year, Weisansal won the vice presidency and Nowocien was appointed to her special director role. By camping out in cafeterias and parking garages, the committee collected 1,000 signatures within a few weeks. Kaleida management called a few petition-gatherers into investigatory meetings for using company space and “harassing” members. The petitioners maintained that their activities were legally protected, but they moved the petition-gathering online after that. (Kaleida declined to comment on these meetings.) Weisansal emailed the 1,000 signatures to the trustee, to CWA District 1, and to the national CWA leadership in September. However, with the bylaws suspended, the trustee was not compelled to hold a membership meeting, and the caucus received a notice from District 1 deferring to the trustee. The Buffalo General steward said co-workers who signed feel as if their voices don’t matter. LEADERS FIRED Shortly after the petition was sent in, Nowocien and Weisansal got word that they were being investigated again by the employer, Kaleida Health, for similar instances of timecard irregularities, but going back to 2024, spurred by the union’s investigations. Then they were both terminated for 2024 timecard issues. Weisansal thinks the case is weak: he has 16 years of service and no disciplinary record, and was fired just now for a paperwork error he had already communicated to his manager about. Nowocien has 20 years of service at Buffalo General. Now, while Weisansal and Nowocien focus on their wrongful termination cases, other caucus members are continuing to speak up about workplace issues, bring in new members, and push for elections to be scheduled. A third CORHE leader was fired right before publication of this article, apparently for one timecard infraction. Kaleida had already audited timecards for 19 union board members and appointed directors in 2025, and found discrepancies for 16 of them. Labor Notes obtained a copy of the spreadsheet that Kaleida Human Resources sent to the board delineating the errors and the action to be taken by members and employer to remedy the errors. Several of those officers paid back amounts they had over-received, or were compensated by Kaleida Health for 2025 errors, according to Nowocien and Weisansal. No one received disciplinary action at the time, and the comments in the spreadsheet show that management was aware that its timekeeper system was to blame for the majority of the errors. Only Nowocien and Weisansal were investigated for timecard issues prior to 2025. Kaleida declined to comment on its timekeeping system or the process of reconciling errors. It was after Kaleida’s first investigation that Gambini moved, in fall of 2025, to open up a union investigation into timecard issues as well. The board agreed to spend $10,000 on an auditor, but the findings were never released to the board, according to Nowocien and others. However, the president singled out Weisansal and Nowocien, and warned them that union disciplinary action could be coming for their discrepancies. Then in May 2026, just before the trusteeship, Weisensal and Nowocien said that President Gambini encouraged them to resign from the board and forfeit their memberships, threatening that otherwise the FBI and Department of Labor would get involved and that they would be banned from holding any CWA position in the future. They declined, they said, because they had not seen any written charges or specifics about the accusations. Local 1168 has hired two more auditors since October 2025, and members are awaiting the results. Emminger, the mobilizer at Buffalo General, is upset with the lack of transparency and the spending of member’s dues: “They have not been transparent about anything.” REVERBERATIONS AT WORK A smart employer knows: Never waste a crisis. Patients and staff at Kaleida Health may notice the effects of a distracted CWA 1168. “Kaleida is 100 percent capitalizing on this dysfunction to push through changes,” Weisansal said. Converso, the organizer laid off after 16 years, said “if we [Nowocien and Converso] were still there, we would be in the streets with everything Kaleida is doing.” One change includes getting rid of a cardiac monitoring unit and shifting around the responsibility for heart monitoring to circumvent the 1:4 nurse-to-patient ratio mandated by the staffing committee and contract. Emminger voted for the CORHE slate in 2020 and then got heavily involved in the union because of their organizing focus. She says there has been no mobilization since the trusteeship, when before they would have been pushing back against the short staffing. “This tells the employer that staffing is not a priority, and this will harm us in the next contract,” she said “They are taking full advantage of this witch hunt, and the proof is in the department changes and job deletions.” The changes will mean more work for nursing staff and less oversight of patients with serious heart problems, according to Nowocien and former Area Vice President Jennifer Hogue, another of the five removed officers. Kaleida declined to comment. Hogue has been telling members they can fight back against these changes, even without the support of union leadership: “We are not giving the employer a free pass to do whatever they want.” …AND BEYOND But the reverberations also extend beyond Local 1168’s own shops. The union has been an important force in the local labor movement, and especially a support to its sister union, CWA Local 1133. Labor Notes profiled Local 1133’s strike in 2021 at Mercy Health, where it represents 2,000 health care workers; Local 1168 represents smaller units in the same chain, Catholic Health. Though the contract barred them from striking all at once, leaders and staff like Weisansal and Converso were “loaned” to Local 1133 to help build the organizing capacity of the strike, which won safer staffing ratios. “I wouldn’t have survived our strike without any of those three [Nowocien, Weisansal, and Converso],” said now-retired Local 1133 mobilizer Bob Scime. “They were rocks for me personally, and our whole local, and they kept our lines going. I always feel a sense of gratitude to them. “I can say the same thing about Erin [Spaulding, the trustee] when we were on strike, she was a rock too, and Cori [Gambini, the president], too. Sign of the labor movement today, that we’re fighting among ourselves. It’s the members who are suffering for it,” said Scime. The bargaining teams and leaders of 1133 and 1168 have organized for the last few years to line up their contract expiration dates, so any future strikes could be coordinated and leverage power for health care workers in Buffalo. Their next contract expiration is in May 2028, when Weisansal had hoped that Local 1168 would join in United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain’s call for coordinated labor action. As the seasons change, Hogue, the former Membership Functions Chair, is also grieving the loss of an annual tradition: the CWA 1168 Halloween Party. “Normally this is a community where people feel like they belong,” she said.

articles.title: One Step, Then Another
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: This speech was delivered by Jenny HB on October 3rd at CDSA’s Field Day event. The text has been edited for clarity. Comrades, we stand today in a moment unlike anything our movement has seen. Capitalism has developed itself into such a state of chronic dysfunction that even those most deeply committed to the status quo find themselves completely unable to articulate a path forward. As the political mainstream continues to lose the consent of the people, our party grows stronger with each passing day and with the deepening crises we face. We are able to offer a credible alternative to the status quo because, unlike the unprincipled liberal and reformist progressives, we have the ability to understand and engage with the world through a Marxist framework. This gives us not just moral clarity but a coherent structural critique. We are able to identify the exploitation that capitalism inherently creates via the theft of the value created by our labor. We are able to identify the instability created by capitalism’s concentration of power in a tiny fraction of the population, and we see how this concentration leads to wars of imperialism as this class of oligarchs searches for excess profits and new markets. While liberals have been blindsided by the rise of American techno-fascism and its atrocities at home and abroad, we know that this is the inevitable result of our economic system. As collapse approaches, our model of the world holds strong as liberalism falls to pieces. DSA has found unprecedented success by addressing these realities head-on, and our growth is cause for celebration. But it isn’t simply because of our worldview and structural critiques. Change and success come from understanding the material circumstances in which we organize, recognizing our strengths and advantages, and planning a strategy accordingly. By acting in the interests of the whole of the working class, we create the potential for a coalition that encompasses the vast majority of people. That scale and broad appeal is our key structural advantage. Our task is to realize this potential and plan how to harness it to fundamentally change the systems that govern us. Our political system is unequivocally a tool of class oppression, yet it is also terrain on which we can struggle. It can be a tool to harness our mass politics toward building working-class power and a working-class party. The power we gain through political struggle, through electoral victories, is more than just a trophy or a show of strength. It is real, material power. It allows us to change the rules and make the terrain more advantageous for our organizing. We know that elections alone cannot win socialism. We do not and should not limit ourselves to electoral work. Instead, we use political power to strengthen our other efforts. We use it to support, expand, and radicalize labor unions. We use it to organize tenants. We use it to bring our message to the public and raise awareness among the working class of their natural antagonism towards the owning class and inherent solidarity with each other. We use it to make our political system more democratic and more representative. Above all, we use it to build a working-class party that can be an agent for revolutionary change. Make no mistake, though we seek to build power for our party, we stand in service to the working class. That means we also have the responsibility to use the power we gain to visibly and materially improve the lives of the working class. The public has spent decades watching idealistic progressives who promise change and largely fail to deliver. We build and legitimize our party when we harness power for the public good. When socialists make the buses run faster, or hold landlords to account, or freeze the rents, we achieve more than just clout — we earn the chance to change minds and raise class consciousness. When government delivers, people listen. From every position we find ourselves in on the path to liberation, we must take stock of all the avenues of struggle available to us, use the power we have gained along the way to advantage our party in those struggles, and redouble our efforts. Along the way we must also solidify what we have built, building durable institutions that can outlive any individuals. Just as capital creates a self-reproducing superstructure, we must build organizations as clearly defined structures of relations, not ad-hoc efforts of overburdened organizers. Our party is strong precisely because of its potential to sustain and grow itself outside of cults of personality and rigid dogmas. We instead place our faith in the only force that merits it: in the radical participatory democracy of the working class. It is of paramount importance that we guard and protect our internal democracy and culture of openness. Radical democracy also means hearing the voices of those most disadvantaged under capitalism, centering them and their struggles. There is no socialism without Black liberation and an end to racism in every form, and there can be no mass politics without a truly multiracial party. Comrades, we have our work cut out for us. I cannot promise socialism in our lifetimes or that we will win. But I truly believe if real change comes, it will be led by DSA. Being a part of this organization is the honor of a lifetime. Thank you. Solidarity forever! The post One Step, Then Another appeared first on Midwest Socialist .

articles.title: Election Denial Is Now Normal for the Right Everywhere
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: The series of recent elections across the globe have been read as a stinging defeat for right-wing authoritarians, which they are. But maybe more notable is another element: that denial of and efforts to simply reverse unfavorable election results now seem to have become de rigueur for the transnational Right. All four of the major elections taking place in the ten-day period from October 25 to November 3 have seen or are seeing efforts by right-wing politicians to cast doubt on results where they lost or are likely to, and to engineer a way to change them in their favor. In Brazil, right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro — whose father is serving a twenty-seven-year prison sentence for trying to organize a coup when he lost the presidential election four years ago — responded to his own shock defeat by announcing a legal challenge to annul the result over the courts’ last-minute extension of voting hours (even though his own campaign had requested the extension). Flávio has now, Juan Guaidó–style , just declared himself the president from Miami, alleging election fraud (before, confusingly, almost immediately deleting the post and declaring himself the country’s rightful “leader” instead). In Serbia, where the authoritarian former President Aleksandar Vučić was toppled from power after twelve years, there were mounting signs he was preparing to launch a violent coup after badly losing the election, before changing his mind and conceding. By the account of one of Serbia’s own former top anti-terrorism officials, Vučić had “sent 4,000 police and 3,000 thugs to central Belgrade” but was talked down from going through with it by European officials. In Israel, the scandal-tainted and genocidal Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has now engineered an investigation by Shin Bet, the country’s domestic security service, into the unprecedented voter share won by Israel’s Arab parties, having accused them of “stealing” the election. If Netanyahu’s opposition can get over their refusal to form a government with Arabs, they will block Netanyahu from another stint as prime minister. And of course, there’s the originator himself: US President Donald Trump, who has since virtually the moment he entered office last year been carrying out a slow-rolling, telegraphed effort to delegitimize the upcoming midterm election result, as presidents’ parties tend to suffer a setback in midterms. As part of this effort, Trump and, at this point, pretty much the entire Republican Party have incessantly seeded the idea that election results can’t be trusted and that his opponents will “cheat” (even as he’s publicly urged his own voters to “cheat like hell”), and they have done everything from trying to purge voters and preemptively challenging the legitimacy of the Alaska election to reportedly discussing simply refusing to certify election results. Six years ago, Trump’s claims that his 2020 election loss was rigged and efforts to overturn it were read as just the irresponsible sour grapes of one particularly dishonest, erratic politician. (Though let’s give credit where credit’s due: he was technically beaten to the punch in recent years by fellow losers in Indonesia , Ecuador , and especially Bolivia, where in 2019 Trump’s first administration backed the Right’s effort to baselessly cast doubt on and ultimately overturn its election loss through a coup .) But the election-denial movement Trump kick-started and that is now a nationwide phenomenon has become something of a model beyond US borders. This flat-out refusal to accept defeat and simply live in a self-created, alternate reality where the loser has actually won, numbers be damned, has now become standard operating procedure for right-wing leaders. According to the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance’s 2024 report on the state of global democracy, losing candidates rejected the result in 20 percent of the world’s elections between 2020 and 2024, something it calls a “growing phenomenon.” That includes Guatemala in 2023, Peru in 2021, and Brazil in 2022. (To be fair, it’s not always right-wingers — Colombia’s leftist former President Gustavo Petro at one point suspended the presidential transition earlier this year, alleging fraud.) Some of this recent spate of efforts to reverse the democratic process have failed or look doubtful because the victory margin for the winners made them untenable — reportedly the reason why both Bolsonaro and Vučić aborted their nascent attempts to steal the election. We will have to see how Netanyahu’s effort fares. The historic 80 percent turnout from Arab voters will make it hard to invalidate votes, and multiple reports have it that the alleged foreign interference that supposedly led to it was actually small-scale and “not something that hasn’t happened in the past.” But Netanyahu’s play may be to use this to make it politically impossible for his opposition to form a government with the Arab parties. Trump’s efforts will likewise be concentrated on those states where the result is likely to be close — but those, too, could be undermined if Democratic candidates end up outdoing polling in the face of widespread unhappiness with Trump’s presidency. Whatever happens, election denial seems firmly here to stay and is now global. We may end up collectively dodging the very worst-case scenarios of election theft this time. But what happens when future results are close enough or otherwise conducive to right-wing claims of illegitimacy and efforts to overturn? It’s a question the Left now, sadly, has to plan and organize for no matter where one happens to live. articles.title: Bottom-Up Organizing: How We Got Clean Porta-Johns
articles.content: The first day I showed up on the Marriott construction site in downtown Detroit, everyone warned me about the state of our bathrooms. You could smell them halfway across most floors. They were full in 24 hours, urinals were often clogged, and some people had taken to using buckets and hiding them in closets. Every electrician already had the same idea: we wanted the cleaning schedule changed from twice a week to three times. I had a long conversation with the steward about what had been tried. The first instinct of a construction worker is to “drag” (quit), drive over to the union hall, and pick up a new job. As expected, there was a steady trickle of drags, but no improvement to conditions. OSHA had been called and walked the site, only to say that the number of bathrooms was up to their standard. The electrical contractor had been notified, but because the bathrooms were for all the trades, our bosses didn’t feel it was their responsibility to pay for additional cleaning. Our Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 58 contract only gestures vaguely to “sanitary facilities,” and protects us explicitly should we leave the site to find a “sanitary” facility. This clause was exercised regularly, but no one could say for sure whether the boss was even aware we were leaving. A PLAN IS HATCHED I was asked to fill in for the steward while he was out for a few days. When I walked the job to make sure everyone had my number, more than half the conversations touched on the bathrooms. I then introduced myself to the stewards from other trades, who were all hearing the same from their members. We hatched the idea to take the issue above our bosses and straight to the general contractor (who hires out each trade and is responsible for the job site at large). Together we wrote a letter titled “Unacceptable Bathroom Conditions,” which opened politely and assumed the boss was ignorant of the problem. The letter referenced the impact on our work and a widespread feeling that we were not being treated with respect. We reminded him that many of us had decades of experience and were not new to the idea of using a plastic box as a bathroom, but these conditions were exceptionally bad. We suggested that the person responsible for scheduling should use our bathrooms for a week to better assess the need for more cleanings, hand sanitizer, and a wash station. We gave one week for a response. BUT WILL IT WORK? Every worker who was presented with the letter signed immediately. Most people felt like the bosses would just laugh at our demands, but were interested in the idea of swarming their trailer at lunch and forcing them to read it in front of us. We fielded many suggestions, from going straight home after delivering the letter to tipping over porta-johns on our way. We told our co-workers that if our response date came and went without change, we would be coming back around “to have a different conversation.” But first the demand had to be made collectively and clearly. Many of our one-on-one talks were focused on assuring the workers that we would escalate if the letter went ignored: “This is only the beginning.” We warned people about possible counter-strategies from the boss, and stressed the importance of demonstrating solidarity, especially across the trades. We didn’t invite the officers at the union hall or our reps, though we did inform them. “Every member is a steward” has become sort of a slogan for us. IT WORKS In the end we had 105 signatures and roughly 35 folks across four trades who gave up their lunch break to deliver the letter. The contractor read it, was brought outside to look at us, and immediately conceded to our terms. Maybe they didn’t know how bad the bathrooms were, maybe they didn’t know how widely and deeply felt the issue was on site, or maybe they figured it was fine to ignore. All we know for sure is, when even a fraction of us came together, with the backing of three times as many signatures, it didn’t matter if we had the union hall behind us. We are the union, the working people who don’t just walk away from a job which doesn’t satisfy us, and our demands have been met. Kevin Szczesny is a member of IBEW Local 58 (Electrical Workers) in Detroit. A version of this story first appeared in his union newsletter.

articles.title: The US Is Starving Cuba. Will It Invade Too?
articles.author: Kurt Hackbarth
articles.content: On September 25, CBS News announced that it had obtained “exclusive new information” regarding potential US military action against Cuba. According to an Army Reserve memo reviewed by the network, the Pentagon was looking at the possibility of mobilizing police forces, medical personnel, and other units to support such an operation. Vague on details, the conveniently timed piece appeared suited to coincide with Donald Trump’s speech at the United Nations three days prior, where he asserted that his administration was seeking a “fundamental change in the situation” with the Cuban government, which is “failing like never before” and “will fall.” The very night of its report, however, CBS published another article effectively walking it back, quoting a defense expert who claimed that the memo in question should be viewed as a routine planning exercise — one with electoral overtones. “It may be aligned with the interest in trying to inspire the South Florida vote to rally around the administration,” said Florida International University’s Brian Fonseca, “and not necessarily fall into the trap of mismanaged expectations.” Nearly a month later, and with no invasion in sight, the Florida state government waded still further into pre-electoral waters, issuing an arrest warrant against former President Raúl Castro for his purported responsibility in the 1996 downing of two “Brothers to the Rescue” aircraft. Castro was the defense minister at the time. Essentially a copy-paste of a federal indictment unsealed in May, the announcement came some thirty years after the events in question but a mere two weeks before unusually competitive midterm elections, where even some safe GOP seats in Florida, like that of Cuban American hardliner Maria Elvira Salazar, are suddenly at risk. In this manner, after ten months of excruciating suffering and the will-they-won’t-they threat of invasion, the medieval siege of ten million Cubans becomes yet one more political football in the US election season. An Avalanche of Coercion Following the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and his wife, Cilia Flores, on the night of January 3, rhetoric was flying high in Trumpworld that Cuba would be next. “I think they’re in a lot of trouble,” said Marco Rubio on the day following the operation. “Cuba looks like it’s ready to fall,” Trump himself commented on Air Force One the same day. “I don’t know if they’re going to hold out.” A week later on Truth Social, he threatened : “I strongly suggest they make a deal BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE.” Cuban American congressman Carlos Giménez gloated that “Maduro has fallen, [Cuban President Miguel] Díaz-Canel and [Nicaraguan President Daniel] Ortega are next.” Not to be outdone, Senator Lindsey Graham warned : “You just wait for Cuba.” And so on in an orgy of triumphalist bloviation lasting weeks. The invasion, however, did not come. What came instead was a total fuel blockade of the island, a flagrant violation of United Nations Charter Article 2(4), Resolution 3314 Article 3(c), and the rules governing freedom of navigation and boarding on the high seas. A whirlwind of executive orders and State Department directives followed, tightening the screws even further. (This on top of Trump having returned Cuba to the list of state sponsors of terrorism on his first day back in office, reversing a removal the Biden administration had waited until its final days to make.) The administration declared a “ national emergency ” regarding Cuba and expanded sanctions, allowing US authorities to freeze the US-held assets of Cuban officials, government-linked entities, and others. Foreign companies and banks now face sanctions for doing business with designated parties, and military-linked firms such as the conglomerate Grupo de Administración Empresarial S.A. (GAESA) are walled off entirely: even indirect transactions with entities on the Cuba Restricted List are banned. Foreigners working in key sectors like energy, defense, mining, financial services, or security have been threatened with sanctions. Travel rules for US citizens were also tightened, as were visa rules for Cuban officials and anyone tied to the country’s overseas medical and labor programs. Remittances and money transfers were restricted further. And beyond the specific rules, the measures created a climate of legal uncertainty about penalties and compliance costs that scares off commercial activity of every kind, which was very convenient for Washington. The result of this avalanche of coercion has, predictably, been devastating. Hotels and resorts such as Spain’s Meliá and Iberostar , Canada’s Blue Diamond, Indonesia’s Archipelago International , and Thailand’s Minor announced they were suspending service on the island. Visa and Mastercard ceased operations in June. Faltering demand and fuel shortages led major airlines like Iberia to cancel direct flights. Shippers such as France’s CMA CGM and Germany’s Hapag-Lloyd suspended new bookings. Over forty banks have ceased operating. A crisis, in short, that may have broken many populations on its own; but not the Cubans, inured like few to withstanding hardship. “Never before has a sequence of measures been set in motion in such a short period of time that so cold-bloodedly carries out a criminal design of extermination — a policy deliberately aimed at creating shortages capable of suffocating a population, threatening its physical well-being, and depriving an entire people of their means of subsistence,” said Ambassador Johana Tablada de la Torre, deputy chief of mission at the Cuban embassy in Mexico, in an interview. Tablada de la Torre lays out just some of the results of the blockade: the infant mortality rate in Cuba, once the pride of the nation and the best in the Western Hemisphere, has more than doubled to 9.9 per 1,000. Survival for childhood cancer has tumbled twenty points to 65 percent. Some 96,000 people are on a waitlist for operations, 11,000 of them children. “The United States is applying the same formula to Cuba that it applied to Gaza, only without the bombs yet,” she says. “And we can’t rule that out. Their theory is that the blockade wasn’t working because it wasn’t airtight. So if they make it airtight and cut off every source of support, the country has to collapse. The opposite is true: it is thanks to our socialist system that we’ve been able to distribute the little we have.” Tablada de la Torre continues: The idea is to intervene, install a puppet government, and restore the colonial rule that existed before. They’ve succeeded in the first respect . . . in making the Cuban people suffer like never before in their history. The only thing comparable was the reconcentration period under [General] Valeriano Weyler, during Spanish rule, when the people were confined to camps. . . . so they could not support the rebels. That’s the only comparison. But where they have not succeeded is in their main objective. They have failed to bring the Cuban people to their knees, because they have not managed to force them to give up their struggle. Cubans Endure Despite the drastic shortages, life goes on in Havana and elsewhere on the island. The bakers bake; the teachers teach; the doctors treat with what they have, while the scientists in the labs move forward as they can. On the streets, the whir of electric vehicles has replaced the grind and groan of the internal combustion engine. As hours of electricity are both precious and unpredictable, people have taken to leaving a small appliance on in order to be woken up if the power comes back on in the middle of the night. To boost electricity production, the government is banking on two main solutions: First, a China-powered solar revolution that is already producing one gigawatt of the three the country needs to function during peak-demand hours. And second, a developing technology called “ thermoconversion ” capable of improving the quality of the heavy crude oil found on its north coast by reducing its viscosity and sulfur content. Unsurprisingly, the attempt at energy sovereignty has also become a target of Trumpian sabotage, with the Center for Petroleum Investigation (CEINPET) being included in the July round of sanctions, almost three months after the announcement of the breakthrough. The Little Invasion That Couldn’t So where does all of this leave the prospect of an invasion? In short, in a very strange space. In the months since the setting up of the oil blockade, Western media has been on a febrile search for the “perfect traitor” that would hand over the keys to the island and defuse popular resistance. For a time over the summer, on the heels of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to the island, they even thought they’d found one in the person of Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro , Raúl Castro’s grandson and Fidel’s grandnephew. It was not to be. By October, Marco Rubio was forced to take to X to effectively crowdsource an uprising, calling on “those who seek to create positive change in Cuba” to seize the opportunity “through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA.” Not very discreetly, the CIA then took it upon itself to retweet Rubio , translating the text into Spanish, only for the US Southern Command to then retweet the CIA. To cap off the delirium, Donald Trump insisted at a campaign stop on October 23 that “we’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” conjuring up the unlikely image of a warship stopping fifty yards off the coast only for the island’s public to spontaneously raise up its hands in surrender. Meanwhile, polls consistently show the US public opposing an invasion by overwhelming margins . As for the “taking care of Cuba” on the way back from Iran, there are two schools of thought. The first is that the Trumpian debacle in West Asia makes an invasion of Cuba less likely, as it stands to suck up attention, resources, soldiers, and carriers for months or even years to come. The “pink tide” of progressive governments in Latin America, according to this thesis, was at least partially due to the Bush administration’s being distracted by the occupation of Afghanistan and Iraq. But many in the region hold another view, darker and more fatalistic perhaps, but rooted in history and a long-standing study of US character: that a disaster in Iran could actually make such an attack more likely, as the empire will need a smaller enemy to brutalize in order to staunch its wounded pride. The war in Iran is hardly preventing the Trump administration from intervening in country after country in the region as we speak, these people would argue. Although an extended occupation, which is what Cuba would most likely require, is another matter entirely. Despite Trump’s fantasies and the obvious asymmetries involved, a hypothetical invasion would be anything but a walk in the park. “The United States surpasses us in firepower and military technology, but if they lose their minds and make the reckless decision to attack us, the cannons will roar in Cuba, and many of our people will die — but so will many of theirs,” warns Tablada de la Torre.
