articles.title: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.
articles.author: Cory Doctorow
articles.content: The artificial intelligence boom is fueled by an elite wager that software can supplant expensive human expertise. The tech industry and its investors are pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into the technology — Goldman Sachs forecasts that global AI-related investment will soon exceed $1 trillion . At the same time, government regulatory regimes are inadequate and consumer use cases often vague, misleading, or utterly counterproductive. The economics of AI don’t make sense unless one factors in what its backers hope to gain: a way to displace workers. In his most recent book, The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI , Cory Doctorow explains how people have become tools of the machines and the capitalists who own them. Doctorow recently spoke to Jacobin to discuss the rise of AI, the financial conjuring tricks behind the boom, the copyright fight, what it all means for workers — and why the answer to AI doomerism lies in building workers’ rights and public power. David Moscrop People talk about AI all the time. You get through the conversation and realize no one has specified what they’re talking about. So, I want to start with the simplest, most complicated question. What is AI? Cory Doctorow That question implies that you understand the most important thing about AI, which is that we call something different “AI” every five to ten years, and we’ve been doing that since the mid-1950s. You could say AI is the label we apply to anything that is doing something that we currently believe is the unique province of a conscious mind. Then it stops being AI once we realize that it’s doing that without being a conscious mind, and we apply the label to something else. But this new, specific kind of AI is actually really useful and interesting from a class-struggle perspective. It’s useful to understand what this AI does differently from the AIs that preceded it. Before this version of AI, we had something we called symbolic AI. The way it worked was that you’d build a software model of the thing that you wanted to use machine learning on. If you wanted to use machine learning to figure out how to play chess, you would first build a software model of a chess board, chess pieces, and chess rules. Then you would use machine learning — a statistical technique that involves analyzing previous games, running iterations, and asking for human feedback — to try to improve the chess game that the AI could play. What the current version of AI does, this theory-free version, is it swaps out these models of the world for a brute-force approach. This is why we call it theory-free. We take all the stuff in the world we can observe, and we feed it to all the computers we can find, and we ask the computers to find statistical relationships between things to try to understand whether A causes B. And while we all know correlation is not causation, causes and effects are correlated. The problem of correlation and causation is that you might think A causes B, but actually it’s A and A’ that cause B. But A and A’ happen at the same time 99.9999 percent of the time, so we can’t distinguish between them. The answer with AI is to keep adding training data until there are enough examples, even with a thing that only happens one in a million times, that we can actually see that it’s A and A’ that’s causing B and not just A. And we just keep throwing more computing power at it. The weird thing is that we do this for things where we actually know how they work. We know how to play chess, but we ask LLMs to play chess for us. The problem is that, because they’re theory-free, they don’t know what a chess board is. If you ask an LLM to play chess, it will sometimes put a piece on a square where it already has a piece because it doesn’t know that it’s playing chess. It’s just pulling statistical guesses out of a multidimensional array that tries to represent the relationship of every chess move to every other chess move in the training set. So that’s what is going on here. We’re also using it to try and pull out statistical relationships between things whose causality we don’t understand. There are far more things in the world that we don’t understand than those we do, but we can observe what seems like a causal relationship. If you get sick tonight and go to the doctor, you might get a medicine whose method of action is not understood. But we know it works, so we give it to people who are sick. We don’t always wait until we understand it before using it — although we do study it. But here’s the thing: by building a system where we can swap brute force for understanding — so, money for theory — we clear the very last hurdle for finance capital as a source of power. Expertise and money are both unevenly distributed, but money is collected in the hands of people who don’t have much expertise, while expertise is collected in the hands of people who don’t have much money. There is a durable source of power among experts. If you don’t want to work for Arthur Sackler, he can’t make you. And if you’re the only person who understands some abstruse area of pharmacology, Arthur Sackler can’t do research in that area. But Arthur Sackler is very, very rich. When you swap expertise for money, you don’t need to convince the only pharmacologist who understands some narrow area to come work for you. You can just throw money at the problem. This is why the AI industry raised a trillion dollars this year on $50 billion revenue: because the finance sector is in love with the idea of a technology where money can be substituted for expertise. The Brief Life of the Big-Firm Wage Premium David Moscrop In your latest book , you describe this dynamic as a reverse centaur — “a machine that uses a human being as its assistant” instead of the other way around. How did we end up on the other half of this thing? Can we flip it back around? Cory Doctorow That dynamic is intrinsic to this kind of AI, in the sense that this kind of AI is really, really expensive and only starts to make money if you can displace a lot of high-wage labor. And this is another area where we have to be really careful to be good materialists and distinguish the sizzle from the steak. Pauperizing commercial artists, pornography performers, and taxi drivers is not a way to recoup the expense associated with training AI. These companies are not doing this to get rich. They’re doing it to demonstrate how awesomely powerful the AI is. No language on earth contains the phrase “as rich as a taxi driver.” Replacing Uber drivers who supply the cars, insurance, depreciation, fuel, and the cost of shampooing vomit out of the backseat with expensive robots that you own doesn’t pencil out — unless your goal is to say, “If we can replace taxi drivers, imagine what we can do to accountants, lawyers, doctors, teachers, radiologists, nurses. And especially people who work in fields where you are legally obliged to tell your boss to f-ck off if they tell you to commit a crime, like medicine, finance, education, and so on.” That’s what has them so excited. We got here because they saw an opportunity — in both the narrative around AI and the surprising statistical smoothness of reality that AI revealed — to both scare workers into docility and, in some cases, to replace workers with software. If you can do both, the software doesn’t have to be capable of doing the worker’s job, because you can acquire enough market power to produce inferior outputs that the public is still required to consume. That’s the goal of every monopolist: to raise prices and lower quality, which you can only do if you have market power. This is why competition matters more than a lot of leftists think it does. It disciplines firms because they have to worry about competitors. And the presence of competitors makes it more difficult for firms to solve the collective action problem needed to capture a regulator and to capture a workforce. I think some leftists believe that the short-lived and extremely contingent large-firm wage premium, where very large firms with a lot of market share paid their workers more out of the excess profits they generated, was a state of nature, and that we need to go back to having really big companies with enough profit to share with us. That’s not true. That was a highly contingent moment in which the hangover from the New Deal coincided with the first days of monopoly — the post–New Deal monopoly surge. There was enough labor power left to force monopolists to part with some of their ill-gotten booty. But that was never going to be a durable condition, because they were going to accelerate their market power, and that would necessarily dampen labor power. That’s what competition is good for: not as an end unto itself but as a way to shatter the class solidarity of the ruling class. Conjuring Valuations David Moscrop Is the industry in a bubble? You see headlines like “Stock Market Had Its Best Ever Year.” I look at headlines from 1929 and think, I’m not convinced that’s such a good omen. Cory Doctorow It is a bubble. I’m not questioning that it’s a bubble. I’m trying to find the ideological and material roots of the bubble. And as a good materialist, I think ideology is downstream of material conditions. Billionaires don’t like to be thwarted. We can think of billionaire-ism as the pathological state of being angry about being thwarted. We all get called on our bullsh-t from time to time, and sometimes that’s bad because it’s not bullsh-t. But a lot of the time, actually we were wrong, and it’s good that someone was around to call us on our bullsh-t. This is why married people live longer — because there’s someone who can say “No, you’ve got to go to the doctor. No, you have to go and you have to stop eating that.” Being called on your own bullsh-t is good, but billionaires are in a pathological condition of not wanting to be called on theirs. I also think there’s this other material story about the bubble. Growth stocks have much higher valuations than mature stocks, not because of superstition or a commitment to growth, but because a share is a claim on future earnings. Growing companies have more future earnings than stable ones. Highly valued stocks are also highly liquid, and so they can be used as a substitute for cash. If you want to grow by hiring people or buying other companies, you can use shares to do that if your company’s stock is highly liquid — which is to say, if it’s growing. Shares are really nice from a firm’s perspective because you can make them endogenously by typing zeros into a spreadsheet, whereas money is something you don’t get to make endogenously without being arrested. You have to get it from banks or investors or creditors or customers. So, firms don’t want to reach the point where markets view them as mature, because they lose that special advantage, and they also lose a ton of their valuation. If you cease to be a growth company, your valuation should have an earnings multiple commensurate with that of a mature company, which is something like 10 percent of the price-to-earnings ratio of a growth company. That means that you become 90 percent poorer the day the market decides you’re not growing anymore. And I know we say, “Oh, endless growth is the ideology of a tumor,” but it’s not ideological to not want to be 90 percent poorer. That is a purely material phenomenon. On the one hand, you have a narrative need to tell a story about how a company that has undeniably saturated its market — Google has a 90 percent search market share; it has saturated the market — is going to grow into some adjacent sector. It could be one that we can all point to and agree exists like, “Oh, we’re doing Google Plus, so we’re about to become Facebook.” Or it might be a fanciful one that you have to convince people might exist, like Web3, cryptocurrency, the Metaverse, or whatever. But on the other hand, because it doesn’t exist, you can make extremely fanciful claims about its eventual valuation. You’re the expert on it because you just invented it. And so you have Morgan Stanley saying, “Mark Zuckerberg’s right. The Metaverse is an $8 trillion play.” Solipsism in the Machine David Moscrop Reminds me of NFTs [non-fungible tokens]. Cory Doctorow NFTs, yeah, which were DOA. AI comes in as the latest version of this. The question isn’t “Is there an AI bubble?” There’s an AI bubble for the same reason that there was a cryptocurrency bubble. The question is “Why is the AI bubble so much bigger?” On the one hand, it’s so much bigger because the computer science is more real. We should not underestimate how surprising it is to discover the degree of statistical regularity in the universe with this theory-free AI. The fact that you can have a thing that closely resembles a conversation with a thinking person just by guessing words is legitimately remarkable. But it doesn’t tell us anything about consciousness — or, at least, that’s not what I think it’s telling us. What I think it’s telling us is that there’s more statistical regularity than our brains would guess without an instrument, in the same way that our brains guess wrong about all kinds of things. Your brain guesses how long you’ve been waiting in line: “I’ve been here for an hour.” Then you look at your watch, and it’s only been ten minutes. We persistently underestimate how regular things are, and the only way we can discover that is by having this thing that ingests a lot of data and then makes guesses. It’s cool; it’s interesting. I think philosophy departments can dine out on this for the next fifty years. But it wasn’t worth a trillion dollars. So, that’s part of the reason the bubble is so much bigger: the computer science is real, and it discovered an interesting fact about the universe in a way that none of that other stuff did. Blockchains are also real; they’re just not as interesting. The number of applications for that kind of slow database rounds to zero. It’s money laundering, gambling, ransomware. That’s sort of it. It’s just not all that valuable, whereas this AI stuff is much more interesting. But the other piece is the ideological one that I alluded to at the beginning: billionaires are very excited about the idea of a means of swapping money for expertise. I think that’s because being a billionaire also means being a solipsist. You can’t make a billion dollars and hurt people in the way that you must in order to make a billion dollars if you think other people experience hurt the way you do. To aspire to a world in which 99.999 percent of the world receives no moral consideration is to aspire to solipsism. AI is a very solipsistic technology. It’s a technology that sort of implies that everyone else is just a bot. If everyone else can be replaced by a bot, then in some sense, everyone else is a bot. David Moscrop Is this version of AI destined to be commodified? AI companies want to rent intelligence back to us by the meter, using content we’ve created. Does data necessarily become a commodity? Cory Doctorow The problem is, I think neither of those things are going to work. Selling intelligence as a service requires that the AI companies remain in business. They’re spending a trillion dollars to make $50 billion. Their unit economics just suck. So, let’s take a little detour into just how sh-tty a business AI is. They’re spending a lot of money to make a little money. That’s not unusual. You spend a lot of money and make a railroad, then make it up by operating the rail carriages over the rails. But there’s a lot of problems with this analogy. In the case of AI, the unit economics — the cost of running the rail carriages over the rails — suck. They lose money on every rail carriage. Every customer they acquire makes them poorer. Every time that customer comes back to use their product, it makes them poorer again. Every version of AI, every new improvement in AI, loses more money than the previous one. And the depreciation schedule sucks. They’ll tell you that they need to upgrade the hardware every five years. They’re actually upgrading it every two to three years, which is wild, because that’s just accounting fraud. If you’ve got assets on your book that you are treating internally as though they’re worthless, but you’re telling the market and your investors that there’s still 40 percent of their value left, then calling that accounting fraud is doing violence to accounting fraud. It’s just terrible. And it matters because even five years of $50 billion in annual revenue wouldn’t be enough to recoup a trillion-dollar investment. But their unit economics are not improving. They keep claiming they’re improving. They keep saying, “Well, the cost of inference” — which is the operating expense — “is going down.” It’s not. Fun With Accounting David Moscrop How does the inference model work? Cory Doctorow So, you have training and you have inference. Training is when you ingest all the data, and you find its statistical relations. Inference is like when some chud goes to Grok and says, “Make me Sonic the Hedgehog, but with giant tits.” They keep saying inference is getting cheaper, but it’s not. And when you look at the balance sheets, you discover that they’re doing the world’s sweatiest tricks to hide this fact. Ed Zitron is quite a good and attentive and detail-oriented watcher of AI. Someone leaked him a copy of OpenAI’s balance sheet, and I can’t think of anyone better to leak to because this is the guy who’s going to go over it as closely as you can imagine, with absolute obsessive detail. He reports that the inference line is a small sum of money. But he also reports that if you keep running your finger down the balance sheet, you get to the marketing budget and find that OpenAI claims to spend more on marketing than Coca-Cola. Coca-Cola has three global marketing agencies with offices in every major city and billboards on every corner. If you want to know whether Coke is really spending money on marketing, you can verify it just by counting billboards on corners and noses in offices. But there is no evidence that OpenAI is spending that kind of money on marketing. Ed’s thesis, which I think is completely true, is that they’re just calling the inference they give away a marketing expense. But that doesn’t make it not an inference expense. That’s like saying “Oh, it’s not a bald spot. It’s a solar panel for a sex machine.” It’s still a bald spot. These companies don’t have a way to rightsize their balance sheet. And even if they did — and this is where commodification comes in — the switching costs are really, really low. When Anthropic started overtaking OpenAI, everyone just went to ChatGPT and said, “Package up all of my data in a format that’s easy for Claude to understand.” And then, they deleted their OpenAI accounts, opened Claude accounts, and started paying there. It’s like if you finish building the Canadian Pacific Railway and turn around, and someone has just put down another set of tracks next to your tracks and their trains are 20 percent faster, and you haven’t run a single goddamn carriage over your tracks yet. So, you’ve got to start building your own set of tracks again. And this is where the open-source, open-weight models come in. The Chinese are taking low-end hardware and open models, and they’re doing something called distillation. That’s when you methodically query Claude and ChatGPT, then use the answers to train your own model without doing the original training. They can’t stop that. The idea that they’re going to be able to charge rent forever on inference requires, for example, that they cook up a giant scare about how their word-guessing program is about to become God and kill us all because their hacker bot escaped containment. Then they get the US federal government, on the one hand, to make it legal for them to all agree to stop doing R&D — which would otherwise be a flaming antitrust violation — and on the other, to ban all the Chinese models. Right on schedule, they’ve done that. But it’s not going to work. Copyright Won’t Save Us David Moscrop What about the copyright-maximalist response to LLMs training on what we create? Does that further commodify intellectual and creative output? Cory Doctorow First of all, the value of your data for training rounds to zero. All we’re doing is creating a crazy version of markets in which affluent people can afford to keep their data out of the model, while poor people accept a pittance — far less than it’s going to hurt them to have their data in the model — and then that data is used in ways that harm them. The problem with copyright is that it’s not a labor right. Artists are told that it’s their primary mechanism for defending their labor rights, but it’s a property right. They call it intellectual property. Think about it: property rights are fully alienable. If you’re bargaining into a market of five publishers, and four studios, and three labels, and two app companies, and one company that does the ebooks and audiobooks, having more rights just means you have more to bargain away for the same price. Copyright has expanded for fifty years. Copyright payments have not. The copyrights required as a matter of boilerplate contract by this highly concentrated monopsony that we sell our creative labor to are just 100 percent of all the rights we’ve ever been given. And every time we get a new right, the standard deal expands. The Hollywood writers were not on strike against Anthropic and OpenAI. They were on strike against the studio bosses, who want to replace Hollywood writers with AI and who are also suing AI companies over copyright. If they win that right, you can kiss goodbye to the socially productive activities that we do that resemble AI training. If you can’t scrape the web anymore, you can’t make a record of what CBS looked like before Bari Weiss took over. If you can’t publish factual assertions, you can’t publish factual assertions gathered from large corpuses — like how chuddy CBS is now that Bari Weiss is running it, what racial slurs they’re using, how many articles are being written by people of color, or whatever you want to name. That all goes out the window if we create an exclusive right to make transient copies of works for the purpose of analysis, perform analysis on them, and then to publish the results. Copyright does not currently restrict those activities to block AI training; you would have to make them restricted by copyright. Then bosses in the extremely concentrated creative labor markets would just acquire those rights as a nonnegotiable condition of employment. They would use them to train chatbots and then fire your -ss and replace you with those sh-tty chatbots that hallucinate because they’re just doing statistical extrapolation. We would then have inferior outputs, worse wages, and a political environment in which it is even harder to hold rich and powerful people to account. If we build out labor rights, privacy rights, human rights, and consumer rights, which are the good rights, and relegate property rights to where they belong — to those things that are so worthless that we can put a price tag on them — then we actually have a chance against AI. articles.title: Occupation of Palestine Will Continue
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the past, many Palestinians and Arabs followed Israeli elections closely. They did so not because they entertained illusions that a Zionist leader would deliver peace and justice, dismantle the occupation or remove illegal settlements. Rather, they feared that some Israeli leaders were worse than others. They hoped to avert the worst-case scenario. Over time, however, that distinction gave way to the belief that all Israeli leaders were essentially the same. This is not pessimism. It is experience. Consider, for example, the expansion of illegal Jewish settlements during the Oslo peace process under Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. Between 1992 and 1995, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank, excluding East Jerusalem, increased from 111,673 to 140,235 – a rise of more than 25 percent, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, drawing on Israeli statistical records. The same pattern continued under the Labor government of Ehud Barak. Within his first six months, Barak’s government issued tenders for 3,196 settlement housing units, exceeding the annual average under his right-wing predecessor, Benjamin Netanyahu. Related: Empty Stadiums, No Accountability: Israel and the Sports Boycott When Naftali Bennett formed a coalition government in June 2021 that included the Arab party Ra’am, settlement expansion continued unabated. According to Peace Now, the Bennett–Lapid government advanced plans for 7,292 settlement housing units during its first year, a 26-percent increase over the annual average recorded under previous Netanyahu governments. The settlements are themselves a driving force behind the occupation. They require land, and therefore land confiscation; protection, and therefore an expanded military presence; water, roads and infrastructure, and therefore the appropriation of Palestinian resources. Together, these elements deepen dispossession and generate further Israeli violence. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the West Bank contained 645 Israeli settlement sites, outposts and other occupation installations by the end of 2025, including 350 settlement outposts. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission reported that Israeli authorities targeted approximately 29,335 dunums of Palestinian land through declarations of so-called “state land” between October 2023 and August 2026—one of the largest waves of such land appropriation since Oslo. By September 2026, the Commission had also documented the advancement or consideration of plans for more than 18,000 additional settlement housing units across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. Alongside this expansion is the violence unfolding across the West Bank. By the end of 2023, the West Bank had experienced its deadliest year for Palestinians since the UN began systematically recording casualties in 2005. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented 23,827 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinians and their property during 2025 alone. In the first seven months of 2026, settler attacks increased by 63 percent compared with the corresponding period of the previous year. Related: Beyond Israeli Apartheid: Why Britain's Greens Are Challenging Zionism Itself Typically, this violence, carried out by the Israeli occupation army and armed illegal settlers, is contextualized within the ongoing genocide in Gaza. But violence in the West Bank also serves another purpose beyond collective punishment: the confiscation of Palestinian orchards, the annexation of land, the expansion of settlements and the crushing of Palestinian resistance, including nonviolent opposition to this colonial enterprise. Any Israeli candidate in the October 27 elections who supports settlement expansion does so with full knowledge of its consequences: further dispossession, military occupation, annexation and violence. The difference between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and politicians presented as less extreme, is often one of language, strategy and timing. Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, for example, openly supports the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, despite his reputation as a more ‘moderate’ alternative to Netanyahu. What, then, about Gaza? Who among Israel’s leading political figures is promising to end the genocide, lift the siege, ensure unrestricted humanitarian aid, restrain the army or investigate violations of international law? None. Israeli media have spent the past three years reporting on major disagreements between the government, military establishment, intelligence agencies and political opposition over what should happen in Gaza. Yet, Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas’ rule in Gaza within 18 months of taking office, whether through the Trump framework or through continued war. For his part, opposition leader and former Prime Minister Yair Lapid has proposed placing Gaza under Egyptian administration for 15 years, effectively shifting responsibility for Israel’s actions onto Arab states. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, meanwhile, supports continued Israeli military control until Palestinian groups are disarmed. The disagreement, therefore, is often over how Israel should achieve its objectives, rather than whether those objectives should change. Other major disagreements primarily concern Israeli society: the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, judicial reform, accountability for the failures of October 7. But these disputes should not be confused with the questions that matter most to Palestinians. If Netanyahu succeeds in forming another right-wing coalition, the policies of occupation, settlement expansion and military confrontation will continue, potentially with renewed momentum. If Israel produces a broader coalition, its members may reach compromises over judicial reform, conscription and other domestic disputes. The occupation, however, is unlikely to become the central point of disagreement. More troubling still, even a government leaning toward the center-left might succeed in presenting Israel to the international community as a country ready to move beyond the image it acquired during three years of genocide, without fundamentally changing its conduct on the ground. The international community must therefore remain vigilant. It cannot allow a future Israeli government to present itself as a peacemaker, or sell the illusion of a newly reformed Israel, while continuing to invest in settlements, occupation, war and genocide. The Palestine Chronicle

articles.title: No Kings Protest I Missed
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Yes, I’ve done this twice before, both times in 2025. Consider this my third (post-)No Kings Day piece, which, like the previous ones, won’t appear until days after that protest holiday (of sorts) goes down in history. Unfortunately, in the latest version, there will be a distinct emphasis on the “no.” The news coverage of the most recent No Kings Day appeared significantly more subdued than in the past and the marches and rallies that day seemingly (or at least reportedly ) were smaller than once upon a time. It evidently mattered not at all that we are now in a world where kingships (a politely outmoded word for dictatorships or autocracies) seem to be spreading. After all, two of the three greatest powers on the planet, the United States and Russia, certainly seem to have moved toward modern-day versions of kings with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, and the third one (Xi Jinping of China) isn’t exactly an elected leader. As it turned out, my own version of No Kings Day reportage has put an emphasis on that “no” and may have proven all too personally symbolic of the moment we’re now in. Once upon a time, I went to the huge No Kings demonstrations/marches in New York City where I live and recorded and wrote about them in my own fashion. As I put it in October 2025 about the previous one I attended, “Yes, in the ever more ominously unsettled (dis-)United States of Donald J. Trump, I recently went to the ‘hate America’ rally in New York City. Or at least that’s what Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives Mike Johnson insisted it was. Who knew that so unbelievably many Americans, millions of us across the United States, would “hate” this country enough to go out and march in the recent No Kings demonstrations, even in places where we might have feared being in distinct danger from the troops of “our” president? In the days before the latest No Kings demonstrations, no matter whom I talked to or where they lived, they seemed to be planning to go to their local version of that march/rally....” However, in the days before the latest NKD (if you don’t mind my now abbreviating it), nobody in the Trump administration or among the Republicans in Congress had a nasty thing (or even anything) to say about it as far as I could tell. For that matter, just about no one I knew said much of anything about it either or was making plans to attend one of the NKD events in New York City. I did, however, prepare for it myself in what has become my usual fashion. I carefully pocketed a couple of pens and the very modest-sized notebook that I had already used when I last interviewed and chatted with people (and scribbled down their endlessly inventive protest signs) at the No Kings rally I attended in October 2025 and about which I wrote a piece for TomDispatch (which I was then still running). This time around, however, this 82-year-old guy was remarkably unprepared for what turned out to be—in terms of weather—the first real fall day in a New York City that had been warm as hell until that very moment on this ever-warming planet of ours. When I stepped out just in time (I hoped) to catch the scheduled beginning of the rally at one of the protest sites in downtown New York City, I was underdressed and found myself almost shivering and chilly as hell (or do I mean as a piece of food in an icebox). I had, of course, checked (I’d like to say carefully but evidently not) online to find the nearest No Kings protest to my apartment. Buy the Book Then, walking to the subway to head down to it, I experienced a first. A nearly all-white pigeon just about flew into me, its wing grazing my right jacket sleeve. I considered it a sign (but of what I hadn’t the faintest idea). I then ran into an acquaintance on the subway platform, where on such days I would usually begin my coverage by writing down all the protest signs people on the subway were carrying to one of the demonstrations. On this day, however, I saw not one single homemade sign in anyone’s hands on the subway car I was riding in or in the station. She and I went downtown together until the train stopped at 57th Street (where she was also going) and we climbed the stairs to Columbus Circle, where I’ve often enough begun marches in the past. Here, however, was the strange thing: when I stepped out, it was early afternoon in New York and that busy circle in the heart of Manhattan did indeed have any number of people passing to and fro on it, but there wasn’t a protest sign in sight or the typical cluster of demonstrators gathering for the start of any march. I circled that circle carefully, asking random people repeatedly about the No Kings march, but no one knew a thing. Finally, I came across an older fellow (like—hint, hint—someone I know all too well—and I mean myself, of course) and he pulled out his cell phone to check on the nearest march and showed me that I had ended up in the wrong place entirely. And then, strangely depressed and shivering in the chill, I walked back to the subway station and headed home. Let’s hope I do better at the next No Kings Day demonstration, since, barring an act of nature, we’re all too likely to have both King Donald and me around for (at least) two more years. The Symbol (Beyond All Symbols!) of Decline and Fall In some strange fashion, however, my experience came to seem to me like the perfect protest moment in Donald Trump’s misbegotten version of America, where nothing turns out right anymore. If I had made a sign, I think it might have said: “This Land Is (Not) My Land” (or the world version of the same), since these days that’s the way it increasingly feels to this old man. When I finally got back home, irritated at myself and thoroughly protest-less, and thought about what I had just experienced, it seemed like the perfect personalized protest symbol of Donald Trump’s America. After all, whether you’re trying to protest or not, nothing really seems to be going well in this country (or this world) of ours, does it? I mean, how the hell did my land ever get him a second time around? We’re talking—and I don’t care what you think of him—about a madman running what had not so long ago been the most powerful country on Earth. Someday, if we’re all still around on this ever-stranger planet of ours, he will undoubtedly be remembered as the symbol (beyond all symbols or, in noise terms, do I mean cymbals?) of decline and fall—not just of the most powerful nation on the planet but (no small thanks to him) of the planet itself (at least as a livable place for humanity). Honestly, in this day and age, on this ever more disturbed and overheating world of ours, how could a near majority of Americans have re(yes re !)elected a man who denies that even the most obvious planetary changes are actually happening. In truth, it’s beyond madness. Or rather, I mean: he’s beyond madness and so, increasingly, is this world of ours. At some deep level, none of this makes any sense whatsoever to me anymore. Climate change is not exactly a hard phenomenon to grasp, and a president of the United States who is determined to deny reality at such a basic level, in some ways the most basic imaginable, seems (or at least should seem) beyond comprehension. And yet here—and nowhere else—we are now, even if I can’t quite take it in. I mean this is simply not the world I ever would have wanted to leave to my children and grandchildren. And yet, welcome to Donald Trump’s planet Earth. Tom's Substack

articles.title: Israel kills six Palestinians in Gaza on eve of announcement of election results
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: The Israeli military intensified its deadly attacks on Palestinians in different parts of the Gaza Strip in the last 24 hours that preceded the announcement of the Knesset election results, which are expected by the morning of Friday, October 30. Read more: Israel’s elections: all roads lead to genocide At least six Palestinians were killed and dozens of others wounded in Israeli strikes that targeted different areas of the war-torn enclave. The fatalities include four government employees , who were killed in an Israeli strike on the Ministry of Economy in the Al-Mawasi area, west of the southern city of Rafah. Thirty others were wounded in the same offensive. The Gaza-based government media office condemned the assault in a statement published on Telegram, describing it as “a new crime and a horrific massacre that targeted a group of civilian public-sector employees.” It added that “targeting government teams and civilian public employees is part of the organized crime that the Israeli occupation has practiced, and a malicious exposed attempt to push towards chaos and disorder by undermining the work of government crews and institutions, which seek to maintain the stability and safety of society.” Meanwhile, two people were killed and several others were wounded when an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle near the entrance to the Al-Maghazi refugee camp, in the central Deir al-Balah Governorate. The latest deaths take the toll of people killed by Israel in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire deal was reached in October 2025 to more than 1,574 people, with 5,867 others wounded, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry also reported that at least 74,570 people have been killed since Israel started its genocidal aggression on the besieged strip in October 2023.

articles.title: The world once again calls for an end to the US blockade on Cuba
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Last Wednesday, October 28, the United Nations General Assembly voted (for the thirty-fourth time) in favor of ending the economic and commercial embargo – which many refer to as a blockade – that the United States has unilaterally imposed on Cuba for more than sixty years. With 130 votes in favor, 17 against, and 25 abstentions, the international community once again demanded that the United States end an embargo that has caused unimaginable hardship for the Cuban people and has slowed the Caribbean nation’s development. One of the countries that voted against the embargo was South Africa, whose ambassador emphasized his concern about the negative consequences the Cuban people are suffering as a result of Washington’s decisions. He also called for Cuba to be removed from the list of countries that allegedly sponsor terrorism, a designation that prevents many companies from doing business on the island. In recent years, the Cuban Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denounced that high-level US diplomats had pressured several of its partners to vote against such resolutions concerning the embargo on Cuba, under threat of serious consequences. The denunciation was repeated this year by Cuba’s top diplomat. Despite these efforts, the overwhelming majority of countries once again called on the United States to end the embargo. Washington appeared to have successfully influenced only its closest allies (those fully aligned with its geopolitical ideology) to vote against it. Thus, among the countries that voted against the resolution are several signatories to “Shield of the Americas,” the new international military initiative led by Washington, to which several right-wing and far-right governments in Latin America have aligned themselves. For its part, the UN news portal reported : “The Assembly expresses its concern that, after decades of votes and appeals, the measure remains in force and continues to negatively affect the Cuban population and Cuban nationals residing abroad, without the expectations of economic normalization having been met.” A multimillion-dollar blockade According to Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez , Cuba’s annual losses are estimated at about 8 billion dollars. The total economic losses since the embargo began amount to the astronomical figure of 178 billion dollars, which is a huge sum considering the relatively small size of a country with a population of 10 million. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez on October 28, showing a calculation of economic losses from the blockade since the UN debate began. Photo: Zoe Alexandra In this regard, the US economic and trade embargo – the longest-lasting in recent modern history – has been denounced by Cuban authorities as a perverse mechanism employed by Washington to boycott, almost from its inception, the Cuban Revolution, which proclaimed itself anti-imperialist and socialist. Added to this prolonged damage are the recent energy restrictions that Washington has imposed on Cuba. Since early 2026, when Washington targeted Venezuela (Cuba’s main energy partner), the possibility of sending oil to Cuba has been cut off by a unilateral US order; the United States warned it would increase tariffs on any country that sends crude oil to Cuba. Only one Russian tanker managed to navigate the waters and reach Cuba – a resource appreciated by Cubans but one that ran out quite quickly. The Caribbean nation depends almost entirely on petroleum for generating electricity, production, trade, and providing hospital care to its population. Added to this are the difficulties in distributing water and meeting other basic needs of the Cuban people, who are the true victims of a new strategy aimed at overthrowing the revolutionary government. In this regard, the support of the international community – the vast majority of which has called for an end to the embargo, considering it a measure that undermines the sovereignty and self-determination of the Cuban people – provides a platform to remind the world of the situation Cuba is facing. Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel said on X : “Today at the UN, the international community’s overwhelming support for Cuba was evident in its condemnation of the blockade and the US government’s policy of maximum pressure. Most of the speakers, some representing regional blocs, were clear in their condemnation.” He added : “It is a despicable act on the part of the empire’s representatives to claim they are defending collective punishment – which exacts a high human cost – against the Cuban people, in violation of human rights. It is a futile effort. They are not convincing, and they achieve nothing except through gangster-like coercion.” Exchange of accusations between Havana and Washington But the vote was not without controversy. During his address, the US representative to the UN, Mike Waltz, said that concentration camps existed in Cuba where “thousands of homosexuals, Christians, and Afro-Cubans” were allegedly detained. In response to the statement, the Cuban delegation, visibly upset, began banging on the table and requested a “point of order.” When the Assembly president did not respond, Foreign Minister Rodríguez and the rest of the Cuban delegation approached the presiding officers and Waltz and demanded that he stop lying. Cuban delegation calls for a point of order during US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz’s speech. Photo: Zoe Alexandra Following the protests, the Assembly president gave the floor to Rodríguez, who said that Waltz was “blatantly lying” and that his “attitude is disgraceful.” He further stated: “Mr. Waltz is lying again, and I wish him a better future in other roles, but at the United Nations and on the Security Council, his performance leaves much to be desired … He is undermining the dignity of the Cuban people and the Cuban government.”

articles.title: Thousands of farmers march for land rights in India’s Maharashtra
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Earlier this week, thousands of farmers in India’s western state of Maharashtra marched to its capital, Mumbai, and forced the state government to recognize their right to the land they have tilled for years and fulfill their demands. Over 12,000 in number, the farmers, carrying red flags and shouting slogans against the ultra-right-wing government led by the Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), were led by the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS), a left-wing farmers’ union. The farmers were also supported by several other left-wing mass organizations, such as the Center for Indian Trade Unions (CITU) and Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI). The farmers started their march on foot and in hundreds of vehicles from Akole on Monday and were aiming to reach the residence of the state’s Chief Minister in Mumbai, a distance of around 200 km, where they were about to organize an indefinite sit-in to press for their demands. The major demands of the farmers were recognition of their rights over the lands they have been tilling for generations, adequate compensation for crops lost due to this years’ drought and a loan waiver of at least Rs 200,000 (around 2,100 USD) among others. The call for the march to Mumbai came after the government failed to respond to the farmers’ demand during a six-day sit-in between October 21 to 26 in Akole. Before starting to march to Mumbai the farmers also carried out a march in Akole itself. The government initially failed to respond to the farmers’ demand and instead threatened them with police action and sent notices asking them to end the agitation. AIKS responded by saying in its press release on Monday that “people’s problems cannot be made to disappear by issuing notices or resorting to pressure” and announced the march to Mumbai. The farmers marched for two days before the government called for negotiations on Tuesday and later announced an agreement on all major demands. Land rights and drought relief A large number of farmers in Maharashtra and other regions of the country cultivate the land without having any documentary proof of their ownership. The governments often recognize such lands as forest areas or put them under categories which makes it impossible to claim private ownership. This often creates threats of eviction and the deprivation of the only source of livelihoods for millions of peasants. AIKS in Maharashtra has been demanding recognition of the ownership of the peasants on the land they have tilled for generations and has led various successful movements for the same in different parts of the state in the past decade. Earlier this year it led a similar movement in the state’s Nashik district, forcing the government to acknowledge the issue and promise reforms. In addition to the long-term problem of ownership, several of the states in India faced a deficient monsoon this year, affecting agriculture adversely and creating losses to millions of farmers in the country. In Maharashtra alone, the government has declared 265 out of 358 administrative units ( Taluks ) as “drought affected.” Most of the state governments have failed to provide any meaningful relief to the farmers yet. However, under pressure, the Maharashtra government recently announced a Rs 5,000 (around 50 USD) compensation for each farming family in the drought-affected regions, inviting strong reactions from the farmers over the paltry amount. AIKS called the government’s announcement of the drought relief “grossly inadequate” and a “cruel mockery of the losses suffered by the peasantry.” It demanded that compensation must be based on the actual losses faced by the peasants, including a waiver from paying the loans up to Rs 200,000.

articles.title: Meet AI Engineer Who Resigned from DeepMind over “Google’s Complicity in the Gaza Genocide”
articles.content: Several tech workers at Google’s AI unit DeepMind have resigned in protest over the tech giant’s work with the U.S. and Israeli militaries. Last week, DeepMind research engineer Sofia Liguori announced her resignation in a letter to her colleagues titled “Stay Human.” She denounced what she called “Google’s complicity in the Gaza genocide” and the increasing integration of Google’s technology into military and surveillance systems. “I felt I could not, in good faith, send this message of building AI to benefit humanity while ignoring that our company was complicit in a genocide,” Liguori tells Democracy Now! “The problem is that when the focus is on the model capabilities and on the potential for agents 'going rogue,' we are shifting the attention from a specific human choice … which is this unrestrained, unregulated integration of the systems without red lines.”
